    "# Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n",
    "\n",
    "We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n",
    "\n",
    "**Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n",
    "\n",
    "**Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n",
    "\n",
    "**Packages required:**\n",
    "    \n",
    "* MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n",
    "* MDAnalysisTests\n",
    "* [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n",
    "\n",
    "**See also**\n",
    "\n",
    "* [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n",
    "* [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n",
    "\n",
    "<div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n",
    "    \n",
    "**Note**\n",
    "\n",
    "MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n",
    "\n",
    "</div>"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 1,
   "metadata": {

   "source": [
    "import MDAnalysis as mda\n",
    "from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\n",
    "from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n",
    "\n",
    "import pandas as pd\n",
    "# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n",
    "%matplotlib inline"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Loading files"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n",
    "\n",
    "  * CORE\n",
    "  * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n",
    "  * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n",
    "  \n",
    "The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 2,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.271171Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.270526Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.612340Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.612777Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stderr",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "/home/pbarletta/mambaforge/envs/guide/lib/python3.9/site-packages/MDAnalysis/coordinates/DCD.py:165: DeprecationWarning: DCDReader currently makes independent timesteps by copying self.ts while other readers update self.ts inplace. This behavior will be changed in 3.0 to be the same as other readers. Read more at https://github.com/MDAnalysis/mdanalysis/issues/3889 to learn if this change in behavior might affect you.\n",
      "  warnings.warn(\"DCDReader currently makes independent timesteps\"\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\n",
    "ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Background\n",
    "\n",
    "The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n",
    "\n",
    "As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n",
    "  \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n",
    "      (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n",
    "\n",
    "The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n",
    "\n",
    "Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n",
    "\n",
    "MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n",
    "\n",
    "The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n",
    "\n",
    "$$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n",
    "\n",
    "RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD between two sets of coordinates"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 3,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.616996Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.616399Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.621101Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.621515Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "6.823686867261616"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 3,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n",
    "         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n",
    "         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n",
    "         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {
    "raw_mimetype": "text/restructuredtext"
   },
   "source": [
    "It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n",
    "\n",
    "The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. "
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 4,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.624939Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.624300Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.625772Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.626238Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\n",
    "LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\n",
    "NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 5,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.629913Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.629406Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.676739Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:45.677176Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e830164f0>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 5,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n",
    "             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n",
    "             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n",
    "             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n",
    "             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\n",
    "R.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array."

    "``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``."

   "source": [
    "ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n",
    "             kind='line')\n",
    "ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n",
    "\n",
    "The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n",
    "\n",
    "<div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n",
    "    \n",
    "**Note**\n",
    "\n",
    "This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n",
    "\n",
    "</div>"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 9,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.106162Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.105620Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.125735Z",

    }

   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e80561610>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 9,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n",
    "\n",
    "R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\n",
    "R.run()"
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                           'CORE'])\n",
    "\n",
    "ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\n",
    "ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n",
    "\n",
    "You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### Mass"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 11,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.282728Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.282209Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.334373Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.334897Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e804833d0>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 11,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n",
    "                  select='protein and name CA',\n",
    "                  weights='mass',\n",
    "                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\n",
    "R_mass.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights."
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                       columns=['Frame', \n",
    "                                'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n",
    "                                'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n",
    "                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "### Custom weights"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n",
    "\n",
    "First we select the atom groups to make this easier."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 13,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.507691Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.507055Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.512950Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.513619Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "name": "stdout",
     "output_type": "stream",
     "text": [
      "Shape of C-alpha charges: (214,)\n"
     ]
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\n",
    "print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\n",
    "core = u.select_atoms(CORE)\n",
    "lid = u.select_atoms(LID)\n",
    "nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 14,
   "metadata": {
    "execution": {
     "iopub.execute_input": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.517921Z",
     "iopub.status.busy": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.517384Z",
     "iopub.status.idle": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.565239Z",
     "shell.execute_reply": "2021-05-19T05:56:46.565638Z"
    }
   },
   "outputs": [
    {
     "data": {
      "text/plain": [
       "<MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD at 0x7f2e80483490>"
      ]
     },
     "execution_count": 14,
     "metadata": {},
     "output_type": "execute_result"
    }
   ],
   "source": [
    "R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n",
    "                    select='protein and name CA',\n",
    "                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n",
    "                    weights=ag.resids,\n",
    "                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n",
    "                                             lid.resids, \n",
    "                                             nmp.resids])\n",
    "R_charge.run()"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "markdown",
   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n",
    "\n",
    "However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code."
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 15,
   "metadata": {

    }

   "source": [
    "df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n",
    "                         columns=['Frame', \n",
    "                                'Time (ns)', \n",
    "                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n",
    "                                'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n",
    "                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\n",
    "ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')"
   ]
  },

   "metadata": {},
   "source": [
    "## References\n",

# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures
#
# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.
#
# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0
#
# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0
#
# **Packages required:**
#     
# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite="michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011" href="https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite="gowers_mdanalysis_2016" href="https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)
# * MDAnalysisTests
# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)
#
# **See also**
#
# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)
# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)
#
# <div class="alert alert-info">
#     
# **Note**
#
# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite="theobald_rapid_2005" href="https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite="theobald_rapid_2005" href="https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.
#
# </div>

import MDAnalysis as mda
from MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD
from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms

import pandas as pd
# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter
# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline


# ## Loading files

# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite="beckstein_zipping_2009" href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: 
#
#   * CORE
#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain
#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain
#   
# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.

u = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)
ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)

# ## Background
#
# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$
#
# As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} %
#   \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ %
#       (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$
#
# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).
#
# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. 
#
# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). 
#
# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:
#
# $$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$
#
# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.

# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates

# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.

rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align
         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates
         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry
         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates

# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections

# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.
#
# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. 

CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'
LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'
NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'

R = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align
             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup
             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD
             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD
             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference
R.run()

# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.

R.results.rmsd.shape

# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.

# ### Plotting the data
#
# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.

df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, 
                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 
                           'Backbone', 'CORE', 
                           'LID', 'NMP'])

df

ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],
             kind='line')
ax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections
#
# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.
#
# <div class="alert alert-info">
#     
# **Note**
#
# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.
#
# </div>

ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')

R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)
R.run()

df = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, 
                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', 
                           'CORE'])

ax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')
ax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory
#
# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.

# ### Mass

# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.

R_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  weights='mass',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])
R_mass.run()

# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.

df_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, 
                       columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', 
                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

# ### Custom weights

# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. 
#
# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.

ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)
core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)

# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.

R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                    select='protein and name CA',
                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                    weights=ag.resids,
                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, 
                                             lid.resids, 
                                             nmp.resids])
R_charge.run()

# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.
#
# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.

df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, 
                         columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',
                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

ref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)
Cell 6 · markdown

Background

The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_i^{\text{ref}}|^2}} $$

As molecules can move around, the structure $\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^{\text{ref}}) = \min_{\mathsf{R}, \mathbf{t}} % \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left[ % (\mathsf{R}\cdot\mathbf{x}{i}(t) + \mathbf{t}) - \mathbf{x}{i}^{\text{ref}} \right]^{2}}$$

The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of degeneracy: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use pairwise or 2D RMSD.

Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms.

MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the RMSD between coordinate arrays, and Universes or AtomGroups.

The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also be weighted by $w_i$:

$$ \text{RMSD}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}^\text{ref}) = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}i^{\text{ref}}|^2}}{\sum{i-1}^n w_i}} $$

RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class (API docs) allows you to both select mass-weighting with weights='mass' or weights_groupselections='mass', or to pass custom arrays into either keyword.

Cell 7 · markdown

RMSD between two sets of coordinates

Cell 8 · markdown

The MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.

The rms.RMSD class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ref_frame, using the atoms in select to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the select selection is calculated. Then, without further alignment, the RMSD of each group in groupselections is calculated.

A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.

ax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')
Cell 29 · markdown

Custom weights

Cell 30 · markdown

You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This is not a typical weighting you might choose, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value.

First we select the atom groups to make this easier.

Cell 31 · code
ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
print('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)
core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)
Cell 32 · markdown

Below, we pass in weights for ag with the weights keyword, and weights for the groupselections with the weights_groupselections keyword.

Cell 33 · code
R_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                    select='protein and name CA',
                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                    weights=ag.resids,
                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, 
                                             lid.resids, 
                                             nmp.resids])
R_charge.run()
Cell 34 · markdown

You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.

However, again, this is a very non-conventional metric and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.

Cell 35 · code
df_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, 
                         columns=['Frame', 
                                'Time (ns)', 
                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', 
                                'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',
                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])
ax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\AA$)')

Quantify the open–closed transition in five RMSD analyses

The published solver question is below. Reference answers and grading code are separate from solver inputs.

Solver question

autonomous-runs/063/explorer-evidence/native/tasks/autonomous-panel-063/instruction.md

RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed→open transition

Background and objective

You are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. AdK has three domains whose backbone positions move differently around a comparatively stable CORE:

  • CORE: residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214
  • LID: residues 122–159
  • NMP: residues 30–59

All domain selections below are applied to backbone atoms. Here "backbone atoms" means the N, CA, C and O atoms of the protein residues (the standard protein backbone selection); "alpha-carbon" means the atom named CA in each residue; residue identifiers (resid) are the topology's residue numbering, 1–214.

Compute the following root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) results, in Ångström, over the full trajectory (frame indices 0–97; frame 0 is the closed-state starting structure):

$$\mathrm{RMSD}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{ref})=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i w_i,|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}^{ref}_i|^2}{\sum_i w_i}}$$

with $w_i=1$ where no weighting is stated. "Optimal rigid-body superposition" means the translation and rotation minimizing the (weighted) RMSD of the stated fitting group; the translation places the fitting group's (weighted) centroid onto the reference's, followed by the optimal rotation. Where mass weighting is used, atomic masses are those given in the topology.

Inputs (read-only)

  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk.psf — topology (PSF format; 3341 atoms) for both the trajectory and the open-state structure.
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_dims.dcd — trajectory sampling the closed→open transition (98 frames).
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_open.crd — open-state AdK coordinates (PDB 4AKE mapped onto this topology).

The trajectory and the open-state structure share the same topology, so selections produce atom sets in identical order.

Required analyses

A. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value). Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition (unweighted), and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs. Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using all backbone atoms (fitting group), minimizing the (unweighted) backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;
  2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed after that single backbone superposition only — no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.

C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD. Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain as the fitting group, and report the (unweighted) RMSD of that group.

D. Mass-weighted branch. Fitting group = all protein alpha-carbons (residues 1–214), with mass weighting. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the mass-weighted alpha-carbon RMSD of the fitting group;
  2. the mass-weighted RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP — backbone atoms weighted by atomic mass), computed after the same single superposition, with no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering.

E. Residue-number-weighted branch. Same fitting group and procedure as D, but the weight of every atom is its residue number (resid): the fitting-group alpha-carbon RMSD is resid-weighted, and each domain's RMSD is computed on its backbone atoms, each weighted by its residue number, after the same single superposition (no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering). This is an unconventional weighting used here to demonstrate custom-weight RMSD; it is part of the requested result.

In all trajectory analyses (B–E) the reference is trajectory frame 0, and every frame of the trajectory (0–97) is analyzed.

Output files (CSV)

Write these files to the output directory. One row per trajectory frame (Frame = integer frame index 0…97), one row set per file. RMSD values in Å. Only the columns listed below are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored.

  1. backbone_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, Backbone, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis B).
  2. ca_core_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, CORE (analysis C).
  3. mass_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis D).
  4. resid_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis E).
  5. open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv — a single row with column Backbone (analysis A).

All values are finite; no missing values are expected. Rows are identified by Frame, and the frame keys must be identical across files 1–4.

Environment and constraints

Any software may be used (an offline environment containing MDAnalysis 2.11.0 is available for convenience; its use is not required). Execution is offline. Limits: ≤4 CPU, ≤8 GiB RAM, ≤10 GiB disk, 600 s runtime.

Acceptance rules

Acceptance-rule addendum

This addendum defines exactly how submitted outputs are compared. It does not change the scientific question in the task statement.

What is graded, and where

The grader reads only the five declared output files, at exactly the declared paths (relative to the submission output root):

  1. backbone_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, Backbone, CORE, LID, NMP
  2. ca_core_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, CORE
  3. mass_weighted_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP
  4. resid_weighted_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP
  5. open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv — compared column: Backbone

Files must not be nested in any additional subdirectory (for example an extra outputs/ layer below the supplied output root); a file at the wrong declared path counts as missing and fails. Only the columns listed above are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored. Each required column name must appear exactly once in the header row; a missing, duplicated or case-mismatched required column fails. Files must be plain comma-separated CSV with exactly one header row; ragged rows fail.

Row grain, alignment and identifiers

  • Files 1–4 hold one row per trajectory frame. Rows are identified and matched by the Frame column, which must contain integer frame indices. Duplicate Frame keys, missing Frame keys, or extra Frame keys fail. The set of Frame keys must be identical across files 1–4 and must equal the reference file's frame key set (the task's full set of frames 0–97, all 98 frames, every frame analyzed). Physical row order is not compared; rows are joined by Frame before any value comparison.
  • File 5 must contain exactly one data row; its Backbone value is compared directly.
  • Every cell in the compared columns must parse as a finite number. Empty cells, NaN, +Inf, −Inf or non-numeric text fail the affected check. Zero is a meaningful value and must be preserved; it is never treated as missing.
  • Each scientific check compares one analysis branch (A–E) against its corresponding reference file, cell by cell, at matched Frame and column identities. A duplicated, dropped, reordered-by-meaning or truncated frame set is not masked by the numeric tolerance; the multiplicity and coverage of frames is part of the contract.

Numeric comparison rule

All compared RMSD values are in Ångström. For a submitted value v and the corresponding reference value v_ref (same file, same Frame row, same column), the cell passes if and only if

|v − v_ref| ≤ 5×10⁻⁶ Å + 10⁻⁶ · |v_ref|

The deviation is measured from the reference value, and the relative term uses the magnitude of the reference value as its denominator. The same rule applies to the single value in file 5. A submission passes only if every compared cell in every file passes and all structural rules above hold.

Boundary and justification: the compared quantities are ordinary float64 RMSD values serialized as decimal text. The absolute term (5×10⁻⁶ Å) is the floor of the rule: it covers the near-zero frame-0 self-comparison values (order 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ Å, where all correct methods return noise-level values numerically indistinguishable from zero) and the small residual differences between independent optimal-rigid-body-superposition implementations of the publicly stated weighted Kabsch/QCP procedure, which an executed independent NumPy implementation measured to agree with the reference pipeline well inside this floor. The relative term (10⁻⁶ of the reference magnitude, up to ≈1.4×10⁻⁵ Å for the largest RMSDs ≈14 Å) bounds the accepted observable serialization/algebra deviation; it is set so that the accepted output difference remains orders of magnitude below any physically meaningful RMSD difference. The tolerance is a limit on observable submission-vs-reference output differences, not a guarantee that every conceivable wrong method is detected — but any output differing from the reference beyond this boundary, for example from per-domain re-alignment, a different fitting group, wrong weights (mass vs resid), wrong domain intervals or dropped frames, fails.

Because the relative term is 10⁻⁶, output written with fewer than about 7 significant digits (e.g. fixed 4-decimal rounding) may exceed the boundary and fail; write values with enough precision to preserve the computed result (standard full-precision float formatting is sufficient). Values are compared after parsing; formatting/round-trip differences are not separately normalized.

Checks

One structural check covers the five files (existence, column names, frame grain, uniqueness, cross-file frame-key identity, single-row endpoint, finite parseable values). Five scientific checks each compare one analysis branch against its reference file joined on Frame: analysis A (open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv, Backbone), analysis B (backbone_rmsd.csv, Backbone/CORE/LID/NMP), analysis C (ca_core_rmsd.csv, CORE), analysis D (mass_weighted_rmsd.csv, C-alphas/CORE/LID/NMP) and analysis E (resid_weighted_rmsd.csv, C-alphas/CORE/LID/NMP). Missing or malformed files fail the corresponding checks rather than being skipped. Acceptance requires all checks to pass; no partial credit is given. The grader never executes submission code.

Task directories

Read the supplied inputs from /workspace/inputs/. Write all required output files under /workspace/outputs/, using the relative filenames specified above. The working directory is /workspace. Aliases /inputs/ and /outputs/ refer to these same directories.

Deterministic grader

autonomous-runs/063/explorer-evidence/grading/grade.py

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Acceptance grader: RMSD analysis of the AdK closed->open transition.

Compares the five declared CSV endpoints between a reference directory and a
submission directory.  Frame-keyed files are joined on the Frame column; the
single-value endpoint is compared directly.  No submission code is executed.

Usage:
    python grade.py --reference-dir PATH --submission-dir PATH --report PATH
"""

import argparse
import csv
import json
import math
import os

TOL_ABS = 5e-6   # Angstrom, absolute allowance
TOL_REL = 1e-6   # fraction of the reference value magnitude

SINGLE_FILE = ('open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv', ['Backbone'])
FRAME_FILES = [
    ('backbone_rmsd.csv', ['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']),
    ('ca_core_rmsd.csv', ['CORE']),
    ('mass_weighted_rmsd.csv', ['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']),
    ('resid_weighted_rmsd.csv', ['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP']),
]

# declared emission order of the check ids
CHECK_ORDER = [
    'structural_schema',
    'analysis_a_open_closed',
    'analysis_b_backbone_groups',
    'analysis_c_ca_core',
    'analysis_d_mass_weighted',
    'analysis_e_resid_weighted',
]


def make_check(cid, passed, message):
    return {'id': cid, 'passed': bool(passed), 'message': message}


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ parsing
def read_csv_rows(path):
    """Return (header, data_rows); raise ValueError with a reason otherwise."""
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        raise ValueError('file not found: %s' % path)
    try:
        with open(path, 'r', newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig') as fh:
            raw = [row for row in csv.reader(fh)]
    except (OSError, UnicodeDecodeError, csv.Error) as exc:
        raise ValueError('cannot read %s: %s' % (path, exc))
    rows = [r for r in raw if any((c or '').strip() != '' for c in r)]
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError('no header row in %s' % path)
    header = [c.strip() for c in rows[0]]
    data = rows[1:]
    for i, r in enumerate(data):
        if len(r) != len(header):
            raise ValueError('ragged row %d in %s: %d cells vs %d header cells'
                             % (i + 2, path, len(r), len(header)))
    return header, data


def parse_finite(text, label):
    s = (text or '').strip()
    if s == '':
        raise ValueError('%s is empty' % label)
    try:
        val = float(s)
    except ValueError:
        raise ValueError('%s is not a number: %r' % (label, s[:40]))
    if not math.isfinite(val):
        raise ValueError('%s is not a finite number: %r' % (label, s[:40]))
    return val


def _column_indices(header, value_cols, base, needs_frame):
    """Map required column name -> header position once per file."""
    errors = []
    idx = {}
    required = (['Frame'] if needs_frame else []) + list(value_cols)
    for col in required:
        positions = [i for i, h in enumerate(header) if h == col]
        if not positions:
            errors.append('%s: missing required column %r' % (base, col))
        elif len(positions) > 1:
            errors.append('%s: duplicate column %r' % (base, col))
        else:
            idx[col] = positions[0]
    return idx, errors


def parse_frame_table(path, value_cols):
    """Parse one frame-keyed table -> ({frame: {col: value}}, [errors])."""
    try:
        header, data = read_csv_rows(path)
    except ValueError as exc:
        return None, [str(exc)]
    base = os.path.basename(path)
    idx, errors = _column_indices(header, value_cols, base, needs_frame=True)
    table = {}
    if 'Frame' in idx:
        fpos = idx['Frame']
        seen = set()
        for i, r in enumerate(data):
            flabel = '%s row %d Frame' % (base, i + 2)
            try:
                fv = parse_finite(r[fpos], flabel)
            except ValueError as exc:
                errors.append(str(exc))
                continue
            if fv != int(fv):
                errors.append('%s = %s is not an integer frame index'
                              % (flabel, fv))
                continue
            frame = int(fv)
            if frame in seen:
                errors.append('%s: duplicate frame index %d' % (base, frame))
                continue
            seen.add(frame)
            rowvals = {}
            ok = True
            for col in value_cols:
                if col not in idx:
                    continue
                try:
                    rowvals[col] = parse_finite(
                        r[idx[col]],
                        '%s frame %d column %r' % (base, frame, col))
                except ValueError as exc:
                    errors.append(str(exc))
                    ok = False
            if ok:
                table[frame] = rowvals
    return table, errors


def parse_single_table(path, value_cols):
    """Parse the single-value table -> ({col: value}, [errors])."""
    try:
        header, data = read_csv_rows(path)
    except ValueError as exc:
        return None, [str(exc)]
    base = os.path.basename(path)
    idx, errors = _column_indices(header, value_cols, base, needs_frame=False)
    if len(data) != 1:
        errors.append('%s: expected exactly 1 data row, found %d'
                      % (base, len(data)))
        return None, errors
    if errors:
        return None, errors
    values = {}
    for col in value_cols:
        try:
            values[col] = parse_finite(data[0][idx[col]],
                                       '%s column %r' % (base, col))
        except ValueError as exc:
            errors.append(str(exc))
    if errors:
        return None, errors
    return values, []


# --------------------------------------------------------------- comparison
def within_tolerance(sub, ref):
    return abs(sub - ref) <= TOL_ABS + TOL_REL * abs(ref)


def compare_frame_file(fname, cols, ref_table, sub_table, sub_errs):
    if sub_errs:
        return False, 'submission table invalid: ' + '; '.join(sub_errs[:4])
    if not ref_table:
        return False, 'reference table %s is empty or unreadable' % fname
    if not sub_table:
        return False, '%s contains no usable rows' % fname
    problems = []
    ref_keys = set(ref_table)
    sub_keys = set(sub_table)
    if sub_keys != ref_keys:
        problems.append('Frame keys differ from the reference: %d missing, '
                        '%d extra' % (len(ref_keys - sub_keys),
                                      len(sub_keys - ref_keys)))
    n_cells = 0
    n_bad = 0
    examples = []
    for frame in sorted(ref_keys & sub_keys):
        for col in cols:
            r = ref_table[frame][col]
            s = sub_table[frame][col]
            n_cells += 1
            if not within_tolerance(s, r):
                n_bad += 1
                if len(examples) < 5:
                    examples.append('frame %d column %s' % (frame, col))
    if n_bad:
        suffix = ' ...' if n_bad > len(examples) else ''
        problems.append('%d of %d compared cells exceed the tolerance (%s%s)'
                        % (n_bad, n_cells, '; '.join(examples), suffix))
    if problems:
        return False, '; '.join(problems)
    return True, ('all %d RMSD cells over %d frames agree with the reference '
                  'within tolerance' % (n_cells, len(ref_keys & sub_keys)))


def compare_single_file(fname, cols, ref_vals, sub_vals, sub_errs):
    if sub_errs:
        return False, 'submission file invalid: ' + '; '.join(sub_errs[:4])
    if not ref_vals:
        return False, 'reference value for %s is unavailable' % fname
    if not sub_vals:
        return False, '%s contains no usable value' % fname
    bad = [col for col in cols
           if col in sub_vals and col in ref_vals
           and not within_tolerance(sub_vals[col], ref_vals[col])]
    if bad:
        return False, ('value(s) outside tolerance in column(s): %s'
                       % ', '.join(bad))
    return True, ('the reported Backbone RMSD value agrees with the '
                  'reference within tolerance')


# -------------------------------------------------------------------- graded
def grade(reference_dir, submission_dir):
    # ---- read the reference side ----
    ref_tables = {}
    for fname, cols in FRAME_FILES:
        table, errs = parse_frame_table(os.path.join(reference_dir, fname),
                                        cols)
        ref_tables[fname] = (table, errs)
    ref_single_vals, ref_single_errs = parse_single_table(
        os.path.join(reference_dir, SINGLE_FILE[0]), SINGLE_FILE[1])

    # ---- read the submission side ----
    errors = []
    sub_tables = {}
    sub_errs = {}
    for fname, cols in FRAME_FILES:
        table, errs = parse_frame_table(
            os.path.join(submission_dir, fname), cols)
        sub_tables[fname] = table
        sub_errs[fname] = errs
        errors.extend(errs)
    if all(not sub_errs[f] for f, _ in FRAME_FILES):
        base = FRAME_FILES[0][0]
        base_keys = set(sub_tables[base].keys())
        for fname, _ in FRAME_FILES[1:]:
            keys = set(sub_tables[fname].keys())
            if keys != base_keys:
                errors.append(
                    'frame keys are not identical across files 1-4: %s '
                    'disagrees with %s' % (fname, base))
    sub_single_vals, sub_single_errs = parse_single_table(
        os.path.join(submission_dir, SINGLE_FILE[0]), SINGLE_FILE[1])
    errors.extend(sub_single_errs)

    results = {}
    results['structural_schema'] = (
        not errors,
        ('all five files match the required schema (columns, frame grain, '
         'single-row endpoint, finite values)'
         if not errors else '; '.join(errors[:12])))

    # ---- scientific checks, one per analysis branch ----
    if ref_single_errs:
        results['analysis_a_open_closed'] = (
            False, 'reference value could not be parsed: '
            + '; '.join(ref_single_errs[:3]))
    else:
        results['analysis_a_open_closed'] = compare_single_file(
            SINGLE_FILE[0], SINGLE_FILE[1], ref_single_vals, sub_single_vals,
            sub_single_errs)

    for fname, cols in FRAME_FILES:
        cid = {'backbone_rmsd.csv': 'analysis_b_backbone_groups',
               'ca_core_rmsd.csv': 'analysis_c_ca_core',
               'mass_weighted_rmsd.csv': 'analysis_d_mass_weighted',
               'resid_weighted_rmsd.csv': 'analysis_e_resid_weighted'}[fname]
        ref_table, ref_errs = ref_tables[fname]
        if ref_errs:
            results[cid] = (False, 'reference table could not be parsed: '
                            + '; '.join(ref_errs[:3]))
        else:
            results[cid] = compare_frame_file(fname, cols, ref_table,
                                              sub_tables[fname],
                                              sub_errs[fname])

    return [make_check(cid, results[cid][0], results[cid][1])
            for cid in CHECK_ORDER]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument('--reference-dir', required=True)
    ap.add_argument('--submission-dir', required=True)
    ap.add_argument('--report', required=True)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    try:
        checks = grade(args.reference_dir, args.submission_dir)
    except Exception as exc:  # never crash without a valid report
        checks = [make_check(cid, False, 'grader internal error: %r' % (exc,))
                  for cid in CHECK_ORDER]

    report = {'passed': all(c['passed'] for c in checks), 'checks': checks}
    with open(args.report, 'w', encoding='utf-8') as fh:
        json.dump(report, fh)
    return 0


if __name__ == '__main__':
    raise SystemExit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Reference solution: AdK closed->open RMSD analyses A-E.

Uses only the supplied inputs under --input-dir; writes the five required
CSVs to --output-dir.
"""
import argparse
import os

import pandas as pd
import MDAnalysis as mda
from MDAnalysis.analysis import rms

CORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'
LID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'
NMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument('--input-dir', required=True)
    ap.add_argument('--output-dir', required=True)
    args = ap.parse_args()

    base = os.path.join(args.input_dir, 'mdanalysis-rmsd')
    psf = os.path.join(base, 'adk.psf')
    dcd = os.path.join(base, 'adk_dims.dcd')
    crd = os.path.join(base, 'adk_open.crd')
    out = args.output_dir
    os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)

    # ---- A: open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value) ----
    # Trajectory universe freshly loaded, positioned at frame 0.
    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)
    ref = mda.Universe(psf, crd)
    oc = rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,
                  ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,
                  center=True, superposition=True)
    pd.DataFrame({'Backbone': [float(oc)]}).to_csv(
        os.path.join(out, 'open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv'), index=False)

    # ---- B: backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs ----
    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)
    R = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='backbone',
                 groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], ref_frame=0)
    R.run()
    a = R.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'Backbone': a[:, 2],
                  'CORE': a[:, 3],
                  'LID': a[:, 4],
                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}
                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'backbone_rmsd.csv'), index=False)

    # ---- C: alpha-carbon CORE RMSD ----
    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)
    ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')
    R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)
    R.run()
    a = R.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'CORE': a[:, 2]}
                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'ca_core_rmsd.csv'), index=False)

    # ---- D: mass-weighted branch ----
    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)
    Rm = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  weights='mass',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])
    Rm.run()
    a = Rm.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],
                  'CORE': a[:, 3],
                  'LID': a[:, 4],
                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}
                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'mass_weighted_rmsd.csv'),
                          index=False)

    # ---- E: residue-number-weighted branch ----
    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)
    ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
    core = u.select_atoms(CORE)
    lid = u.select_atoms(LID)
    nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)
    Rr = rms.RMSD(u, u,
                  select='protein and name CA',
                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],
                  weights=ag.resids,
                  weights_groupselections=[core.resids, lid.resids,
                                           nmp.resids])
    Rr.run()
    a = Rr.results.rmsd
    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),
                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],
                  'CORE': a[:, 3],
                  'LID': a[:, 4],
                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}
                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'resid_weighted_rmsd.csv'),
                          index=False)

    print('oracle complete: %s' % out)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Task Description:

RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed→open transition

Background and objective

You are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. AdK has three domains whose backbone positions move differently around a comparatively stable CORE:

  • CORE: residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214
  • LID: residues 122–159
  • NMP: residues 30–59

All domain selections below are applied to backbone atoms. Here "backbone atoms" means the N, CA, C and O atoms of the protein residues (the standard protein backbone selection); "alpha-carbon" means the atom named CA in each residue; residue identifiers (resid) are the topology's residue numbering, 1–214.

Compute the following root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) results, in Ångström, over the full trajectory (frame indices 0–97; frame 0 is the closed-state starting structure):

$$\mathrm{RMSD}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{ref})=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i w_i,|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}^{ref}_i|^2}{\sum_i w_i}}$$

with $w_i=1$ where no weighting is stated. "Optimal rigid-body superposition" means the translation and rotation minimizing the (weighted) RMSD of the stated fitting group; the translation places the fitting group's (weighted) centroid onto the reference's, followed by the optimal rotation. Where mass weighting is used, atomic masses are those given in the topology.

Inputs (read-only)

  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk.psf — topology (PSF format; 3341 atoms) for both the trajectory and the open-state structure.
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_dims.dcd — trajectory sampling the closed→open transition (98 frames).
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_open.crd — open-state AdK coordinates (PDB 4AKE mapped onto this topology).

The trajectory and the open-state structure share the same topology, so selections produce atom sets in identical order.

Required analyses

A. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value). Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition (unweighted), and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs. Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using all backbone atoms (fitting group), minimizing the (unweighted) backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;
  2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed after that single backbone superposition only — no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.

C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD. Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain as the fitting group, and report the (unweighted) RMSD of that group.

D. Mass-weighted branch. Fitting group = all protein alpha-carbons (residues 1–214), with mass weighting. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the mass-weighted alpha-carbon RMSD of the fitting group;
  2. the mass-weighted RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP — backbone atoms weighted by atomic mass), computed after the same single superposition, with no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering.

E. Residue-number-weighted branch. Same fitting group and procedure as D, but the weight of every atom is its residue number (resid): the fitting-group alpha-carbon RMSD is resid-weighted, and each domain's RMSD is computed on its backbone atoms, each weighted by its residue number, after the same single superposition (no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering). This is an unconventional weighting used here to demonstrate custom-weight RMSD; it is part of the requested result.

In all trajectory analyses (B–E) the reference is trajectory frame 0, and every frame of the trajectory (0–97) is analyzed.

Output files (CSV)

Write these files to the output directory. One row per trajectory frame (Frame = integer frame index 0…97), one row set per file. RMSD values in Å. Only the columns listed below are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored.

  1. backbone_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, Backbone, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis B).
  2. ca_core_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, CORE (analysis C).
  3. mass_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis D).
  4. resid_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis E).
  5. open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv — a single row with column Backbone (analysis A).

All values are finite; no missing values are expected. Rows are identified by Frame, and the frame keys must be identical across files 1–4.

Environment and constraints

Any software may be used (an offline environment containing MDAnalysis 2.11.0 is available for convenience; its use is not required). Execution is offline. Limits: ≤4 CPU, ≤8 GiB RAM, ≤10 GiB disk, 600 s runtime.

Acceptance rules

Acceptance-rule addendum

This addendum defines exactly how submitted outputs are compared. It does not change the scientific question in the task statement.

What is graded, and where

The grader reads only the five declared output files, at exactly the declared paths (relative to the submission output root):

  1. backbone_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, Backbone, CORE, LID, NMP
  2. ca_core_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, CORE
  3. mass_weighted_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP
  4. resid_weighted_rmsd.csv — compared columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP
  5. open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv — compared column: Backbone

Files must not be nested in any additional subdirectory (for example an extra outputs/ layer below the supplied output root); a file at the wrong declared path counts as missing and fails. Only the columns listed above are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored. Each required column name must appear exactly once in the header row; a missing, duplicated or case-mismatched required column fails. Files must be plain comma-separated CSV with exactly one header row; ragged rows fail.

Row grain, alignment and identifiers

  • Files 1–4 hold one row per trajectory frame. Rows are identified and matched by the Frame column, which must contain integer frame indices. Duplicate Frame keys, missing Frame keys, or extra Frame keys fail. The set of Frame keys must be identical across files 1–4 and must equal the reference file's frame key set (the task's full set of frames 0–97, all 98 frames, every frame analyzed). Physical row order is not compared; rows are joined by Frame before any value comparison.
  • File 5 must contain exactly one data row; its Backbone value is compared directly.
  • Every cell in the compared columns must parse as a finite number. Empty cells, NaN, +Inf, −Inf or non-numeric text fail the affected check. Zero is a meaningful value and must be preserved; it is never treated as missing.
  • Each scientific check compares one analysis branch (A–E) against its corresponding reference file, cell by cell, at matched Frame and column identities. A duplicated, dropped, reordered-by-meaning or truncated frame set is not masked by the numeric tolerance; the multiplicity and coverage of frames is part of the contract.

Numeric comparison rule

All compared RMSD values are in Ångström. For a submitted value v and the corresponding reference value v_ref (same file, same Frame row, same column), the cell passes if and only if

|v − v_ref| ≤ 5×10⁻⁶ Å + 10⁻⁶ · |v_ref|

The deviation is measured from the reference value, and the relative term uses the magnitude of the reference value as its denominator. The same rule applies to the single value in file 5. A submission passes only if every compared cell in every file passes and all structural rules above hold.

Boundary and justification: the compared quantities are ordinary float64 RMSD values serialized as decimal text. The absolute term (5×10⁻⁶ Å) is the floor of the rule: it covers the near-zero frame-0 self-comparison values (order 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁸ Å, where all correct methods return noise-level values numerically indistinguishable from zero) and the small residual differences between independent optimal-rigid-body-superposition implementations of the publicly stated weighted Kabsch/QCP procedure, which an executed independent NumPy implementation measured to agree with the reference pipeline well inside this floor. The relative term (10⁻⁶ of the reference magnitude, up to ≈1.4×10⁻⁵ Å for the largest RMSDs ≈14 Å) bounds the accepted observable serialization/algebra deviation; it is set so that the accepted output difference remains orders of magnitude below any physically meaningful RMSD difference. The tolerance is a limit on observable submission-vs-reference output differences, not a guarantee that every conceivable wrong method is detected — but any output differing from the reference beyond this boundary, for example from per-domain re-alignment, a different fitting group, wrong weights (mass vs resid), wrong domain intervals or dropped frames, fails.

Because the relative term is 10⁻⁶, output written with fewer than about 7 significant digits (e.g. fixed 4-decimal rounding) may exceed the boundary and fail; write values with enough precision to preserve the computed result (standard full-precision float formatting is sufficient). Values are compared after parsing; formatting/round-trip differences are not separately normalized.

Checks

One structural check covers the five files (existence, column names, frame grain, uniqueness, cross-file frame-key identity, single-row endpoint, finite parseable values). Five scientific checks each compare one analysis branch against its reference file joined on Frame: analysis A (open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv, Backbone), analysis B (backbone_rmsd.csv, Backbone/CORE/LID/NMP), analysis C (ca_core_rmsd.csv, CORE), analysis D (mass_weighted_rmsd.csv, C-alphas/CORE/LID/NMP) and analysis E (resid_weighted_rmsd.csv, C-alphas/CORE/LID/NMP). Missing or malformed files fail the corresponding checks rather than being skipped. Acceptance requires all checks to pass; no partial credit is given. The grader never executes submission code.

Task directories

Read the supplied inputs from /workspace/inputs/. Write all required output files under /workspace/outputs/, using the relative filenames specified above. The working directory is /workspace. Aliases /inputs/ and /outputs/ refer to these same directories.

import MDAnalysis as mda
import numpy as np
from MDAnalysis.analysis.rms import rmsd
p='/workspace/inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/'
u=mda.Universe(p+'adk.psf',p+'adk_dims.dcd')
bb=u.select_atoms('protein and name N CA C O')
ca=u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')
for name,a in [('bb',bb),('ca',ca)]:
    counts={d:np.sum(np.isin(a.resids, r)) for d,r in [('CORE',np.r_[1:30,60:122,160:215]),('LID',np.arange(122,160)),('NMP',np.arange(30,60))]}
    print(name,len(a),counts)

def kab_rmsd(x,y,w=None):
    x=np.asarray(x,float); y=np.asarray(y,float)
    if w is None: w=np.ones(len(x))
    else: w=np.asarray(w,float)
    cx=np.average(x,axis=0,weights=w); cy=np.average(y,axis=0,weights=w)
    xc=x-cx; yc=y-cy
    h=(xc*w[:,None]).T@yc
    V,S,Vt=np.linalg.svd(h)
    d=np.sign(np.linalg.det(V@Vt))
    if d < 0: Vt[-1] *= -1
    R=Vt.T@V.T
    xt=xc@R.T+cy
    return np.sqrt(np.average(np.sum((xt-y)**2,axis=1),weights=w)),R

# Compare explicit Kabsch to MDAnalysis rmsd on representative frames.
u.trajectory[0]; y_bb=bb.positions.copy(); y_ca=ca.positions.copy()
for ts in [0,1,25,50,97]:
    u.trajectory[ts]
    for label,a,y in [('bb',bb,y_bb),('ca',ca,y_ca)]:
        m=a.masses
        er,_=kab_rmsd(a.positions,y)
        em,_=kab_rmsd(a.positions,y,m)
        mr=rmsd(a.positions,y,superposition=True)
        mm=rmsd(a.positions,y,weights=m,superposition=True)
        print(ts,label,'explicit',f'{er:.12f}',f'{em:.12f}','MDA',f'{mr:.12f}',f'{mm:.12f}','diff',f'{abs(er-mr):.3g}',f'{abs(em-mm):.3g}')
