    "candidate/analysis.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf.\n# Zipping and <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Unzipping</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Adenylate</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Kinase</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Atomistic</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Insights</span> into the <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Ensemble</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Open</span>\u2194<span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Closed</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Transitions</span>.\n# <em>Journal of Molecular Biology</em>, 394(1):160\u2013176, November 2009.\n# 00107.\n# URL: <a href=\"https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164\">https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009</a>.\n#\n# [2] Richard&nbsp;J.     "trial/reference.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf.\n# Zipping and <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Unzipping</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Adenylate</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Kinase</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Atomistic</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Insights</span> into the <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Ensemble</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Open</span>\u2194<span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Closed</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Transitions</span>.\n# <em>Journal of Molecular Biology</em>, 394(1):160\u2013176, November 2009.\n# 00107.\n# URL: <a href=\"https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164\">https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009</a>.\n#\n# [2] Richard&nbsp;J. Gowers, Max Linke, Jonathan Barnoud, Tyler J.&nbsp;E. Reddy, Manuel&nbsp;N. Melo, Sean&nbsp;L. Seyler, Jan Doma\u0144ski, David&nbsp;L. Dotson, S\u00e9bastien Buchoux, Ian&nbsp;M. Kenney, and Oliver Beckstein.\n# <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">MDAnalysis</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">A</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Python</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Package</span> for the <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Rapid</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Analysis</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Molecular</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Dynamics</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Simulations</span>.\n# <em>Proceedings of the 15th Python in Science Conference</em>, pages 98\u2013105, 2016.\n# 00152.\n# URL: <a href=\"https://conference.scipy.org/proceedings/scipy2016/oliver_beckstein.html\">https://conference.scipy.org/proceedings/scipy2016/oliver_beckstein.html</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">doi:10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e</a>.\n#\n# [3] Naveen Michaud-Agrawal, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf, and Oliver Beckstein.\n# <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">MDAnalysis</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">A</span> toolkit for the analysis of molecular dynamics simulations.\n# <em>Journal of Computational Chemistry</em>, 32(10):2319\u20132327, July 2011.\n# 00778.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787\">http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">doi:10.1002/jcc.21787</a>.\n#\n# [4] Douglas&nbsp;L. Theobald.\n# Rapid calculation of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">RMSDs</span> using a quaternion-based characteristic polynomial.\n# <em>Acta Crystallographica Section A Foundations of Crystallography</em>, 61(4):478\u2013480, July 2005.\n# 00127.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266\">http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">doi:10.1107/S0108767305015266</a>.\n\n\nimport os as _os\n\n_export_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\n_os.makedirs(_export_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\ndf.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"ca_core_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_mass.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"mass_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_charge.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"resid_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)",

Proposed question

autonomous-runs/063/explorer-evidence/specification/task-brief.md

RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed→open transition

Background and objective

You are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. AdK has three domains whose backbone positions move differently around a comparatively stable CORE: CORE (residues 1–29, 60–121, 160–214), LID (residues 122–159) and NMP (residues 30–59). All domain selections below are applied to backbone atoms.

Compute the following root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) results, in Ångström, over the full trajectory (frame indices 0–97; frame 0 is the closed-state starting structure):

$$\mathrm{RMSD}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{x}^{ref})=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_i w_i,|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}^{ref}_i|^2}{\sum_i w_i}}$$

with $w_i=1$ where no weighting is stated. "Optimal rigid-body superposition" means the translation and rotation minimizing the (weighted) RMSD of the stated fitting group; the translation places the fitting group's weighted centroid onto the reference's, followed by the optimal rotation.

Inputs (read-only)

  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk.psf — topology (PSF format; 3341 atoms) for both the trajectory and the open-state structure.
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_dims.dcd — trajectory sampling the closed→open transition (98 frames).
  • inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_open.crd — open-state AdK coordinates (PDB 4AKE mapped onto this topology).

The trajectory and the open-state structure share the same topology, so selections produce atom sets in identical order.

Required analyses

A. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value). Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.

B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs. Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using all backbone atoms (fitting group), minimizing the backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;
  2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed after that single backbone superposition only — no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.

C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD. Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain as the fitting group, and report the RMSD of that group.

D. Mass-weighted branch. Fitting group = all protein alpha-carbons (residue identifier 1–214), with mass weighting. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. Report, per frame:

  1. the mass-weighted alpha-carbon RMSD of the fitting group;
  2. the mass-weighted RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP, backbone atoms weighted by atomic mass), computed after the same single superposition, with no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering.

E. Residue-number-weighted branch. Same fitting group and procedure as D, but the weight of every atom is its residue number (resid): the fitting-group alpha-carbon RMSD is resid-weighted, and each domain's RMSD is computed on its backbone atoms, each weighted by its residue number, after the same single superposition (no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering). This is an unconventional weighting used here to demonstrate custom-weight RMSD; it is part of the requested result.

In all trajectory analyses the reference is trajectory frame 0, and every frame of the trajectory is analyzed.

Output files (CSV)

One row per trajectory frame (Frame = integer frame index 0…97), one row set per file. RMSD values in Å. Only the columns listed below are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored.

  1. backbone_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, Backbone, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis B).
  2. ca_core_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, CORE (analysis C).
  3. mass_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis D).
  4. resid_weighted_rmsd.csv — columns: Frame, C-alphas, CORE, LID, NMP (analysis E).
  5. open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv — a single row with column Backbone (analysis A).

All values are finite; no missing values are expected. Rows are identified by Frame, and the frame keys must be identical across files 1–4.

Environment and constraints

Any software may be used (an offline environment containing MDAnalysis 2.11.0 is available for convenience; its use is not required). Execution is offline. Limits: ≤4 CPU, ≤8 GiB RAM, ≤10 GiB disk, 600 s runtime.

Proposed comparison rules (to validate, not yet calibrated)

  • Same-quantity tolerance: propose an absolute-plus-relative element for per-frame RMSD, calibrated by measuring (i) rerun-to-rerun spread, (ii) independent-implementation deviations (Kabsch vs QCP; float32 vs float64 coordinate pipelines — the reference internally casts to float64 and the in-file notes warn float32 gives errors up to ~1e-3 Å), (iii) unacceptable-output separations. Do not fix numeric tolerances before these measurements.
  • Near-zero behavior: frame 0 self-comparison values are ~1e-7–1e-8 Å in the reference (floating-point residue, not exact zero). Validation must measure how an exact-zero frame-0 submission should be treated and calibrate an absolute floor accordingly. Include boundary rows in the probe set.
  • Incorrect outputs the validation must distinguish (scientific differences, not tolerance cases): per-domain independent re-superposition (changes CORE/LID/NMP columns materially); omitting the reference-centroid translation; backbone vs alpha-carbon fitting groups; unweighted domain columns in the mass branch (narrative suggests this but executed code mass-weights groups — see review; the contract states the executed method); wrong resid ranges (LID 122–159 vs off-by-one); wrong reference (open CRD instead of frame 0).
  • Replay caveats observed: byte-identical replays show serialization stability only. Row order is scientifically meaningful (frame sequence) and must be enforced via the Frame key, not hash equality.

Unresolved choices to settle during validation

  • Whether to also grade a solver-supplied time column against the DCD-header-derived values (currently excluded).
  • Exact CSV column-order strictness (proposed: name-matched, order-agnostic).
  • Tolerance values and the frame-0 numeric floor.

Resource policy

Limits per task_policy: 4 CPU, 8 GiB RAM, 10 GiB disk, offline, 600 s solver and reference timeouts, 120 s verifier timeout; binary reward on all required checks.

Materialize a proposed scientific task from existing evidence

You are a GLM worker building supplied task inputs and a reference solution. Follow the scientific scope in policy and the latest specification. Older exports are evidence, not a requirement to ask the solver for all of them. Do not copy the original function-by-function recipe into the public question.

Submit a complete initial candidate from the supplied source, proposal and recorded observations before using the shell. The controller enforces this ordering: shell commands do not run until a candidate has undergone controlled execution. Use the already executed reference packages and computation for the initial oracle. If execution fails, tool access becomes available to diagnose and repair that demonstrated failure. If the supplied evidence cannot support a candidate, return a concrete blocked disposition instead of inventing missing scientific facts. Successful construction hands off to independent scientific validation; it does not require you to establish numerical equivalence first.

This is construction, not independent scientific validation; a later blind worker performs that check. Prefer adapting the already executed reference implementation. When prior_worker_draft is supplied, reuse its supported code and repair the remaining gaps from source evidence and inspected inputs. Prior execution does not prove its public contract complete. Submit a complete candidate including unchanged fields, rather than rebuilding a separate implementation without a concrete need.

You receive the source, export evidence, replay observations, and the proposed public task together with its private scientific review. draft_ready means a proposal ready for construction, not an approved or validated scientific contract. Read the review before investigating; preserve its established facts and unresolved questions instead of rediscovering them. Notes about later validation are context, not a request to implement that validation here.

Check the proposal against the supplied input observations. Do not assert an input precondition that has not been measured or retain a known unsupported convention solely because the proposal stated it. You may clarify unsupported incidental conventions without changing the scientific target; explain the evidence and each clarification in the rationale. A substantive methodological change requires a blocker, not a silent repair. Leave unresolved numerical equivalence to the comparison stage; do not attempt repeated full independent implementations before submitting a candidate. Grader design and independent-implementation plans belong to later workers. The shell runs in a locked Python environment, offline. /work/reference contains read-only original terminal artifacts. original_inputs identifies read-only original input files and their recorded identities. Work under /work/author. Preserve recorded reference artifacts unchanged. Prefer projecting their existing fields. When policy permits, recover a required scientific endpoint absent from those exports by rerunning its original source computation with unchanged methods, arguments, original inputs and required input state. Keep this recovery separate from the recorded reference, document source locations and state/dependency lineage, and let controlled execution and subsequent independent validation check it. An unnamed or overwritten result alone is not permission to drop a scientific branch. Do not guess missing state, repair source defects, change methods or inputs, add a new analysis, or reconstruct plotting internals. Block if faithful recovery cannot be established. Avoid unrelated upstream work.

Return a complete structured artifact:

  • instruction: standalone solver question with scientific methods, inputs under inputs/, outputs under outputs/, identifiers, schemas and resource limits. No private paths, measured answer values or exhaustive API recipe. Grading tolerances remain pending validation; do not invent them. Keep pipeline status and pending-validation notes in the private rationale, not the solver question. The controller will append the validated acceptance rules before solving.
  • input_paths, output_paths: relative files inside the respective directories.
  • derive_code: Python CLI accepting --source-inputs PATH (JSON manifest of original absolute paths), --reference-dir PATH (original terminal artifacts), and --destination PATH. Create only destination/inputs/ and destination/reference/. Copy original task data byte-for-byte where required, derive proposed supplied metadata by selecting existing fields, and project selected answer fields from existing reference exports. Where policy permits source-faithful recovery, also save recovered endpoints under the new destination with explicit provenance; retain the original reference untouched. No invented answer values, new analysis or changed scientific methods/inputs. Document the source computation, required state and artifact lineage in the rationale.
  • oracle_code: Python CLI accepting --input-dir PATH and --output-dir PATH. Solve the public task using only those supplied inputs. It will run under a separate user without access to reference answers or your working directory. Never embed measured answers, access the original reference, or depend on a hidden cache/author artifact. Use the installed environment; no internet.
  • rationale: private explanation of scope, scientific fidelity, input derivation, possible leakage, output projections and remaining comparison questions.

Validate cell/entity alignment explicitly. Prefer original stable identifiers or explicit composite keys for supplied metadata; avoid making the solver reconstruct an incidental package-specific naming convention when a transparent key can be supplied without changing the science. Supplied intermediate results are reference-derived inputs, not biological ground truth. Retain sufficient identity information without exposing downstream answers. Check claimed input formats and headers against the actual staged files. Inspect the actual input keys and output grain, rather than assuming one source row is one scientific entity. When parsing drops records, distinguish verified metadata and scientifically justified selection from unsupported data loss. Never describe a real observation as a header simply because the reference skips it. Report a source-fidelity blocker when the stated population and actual parsing conflict; do not change the source, input bytes or public population merely to reproduce that defect. If the necessary file observations are unavailable, state the evidence gap instead of inventing them. When several source rows share an entity key, check whether their annotations agree. State the intended multiplicity and any rule for selecting or combining conflicting annotations in the public question, supported by the source analysis. Do not leave these as hidden oracle conventions or choose a rule merely to match saved answers; report a blocker if the source and requested task cannot support an explicit rule. Keep the task scientifically substantial. The oracle may use reference packages; the public task does not require those APIs. Do not silently change the requested scientific quantities merely to fit the saved answers. Report a blocker for a genuine incompatibility.

Submit a minimal complete candidate promptly. The controller executes derivation, verifies exact declared inventories and unchanged original input hashes, then runs the oracle from a clean directory for the supplied reference time limit. It returns runtime/schema failures so you can repair your programs. Successful execution alone does not validate numerical equivalence: a separate comparison stage checks the oracle outputs against the projected reference and tests alternatives/errors. Do not spend this stage constructing a grader, a separate clean-room implementation, or a broad mutation suite. Prefer the simplest faithful oracle, normally using the reference packages already installed: adapt the source computation to the proposed scope and supplied inputs. Do not reimplement those packages from statistical primitives in this stage. A fresh worker will independently implement the public question during comparison validation; do not duplicate that stage here. Still report an actual conflict between the public definition and the reference.

Use disposition: ready or blocked; explain blockers in rationale. Tools are shell, submit_artifact and revise_artifact. Do not claim tests you did not run.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Where the public question frees row order or textual number formatting, do not reverse-engineer those incidental choices just to match file bytes. A later stage compares scientific content under the validated public contract.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

    "candidate/pyproject.toml": "[project]\nname = \"mdanalysis-rmsd-setup\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.13\"\ndependencies = [\n    \"MDAnalysis==2.11.0\",\n    \"MDAnalysisTests==2.11.0\",\n    \"matplotlib==3.11.2\",\n    \"pandas==3.1.0\",\n]\n",
    "inputs/exports.py": "import os as _os\n\n_export_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\n_os.makedirs(_export_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\ndf.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"ca_core_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_mass.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"mass_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_charge.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"resid_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)",
    "inputs/original.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf.\n# Zipping and <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Unzipping</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Adenylate</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Kinase</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Atomistic</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Insights</span> into the <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Ensemble</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Open</span>\u2194<span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Closed</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Transitions</span>.\n# <em>Journal of Molecular Biology</em>, 394(1):160\u2013176, November 2009.\n# 00107.\n# URL: <a href=\"https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164\">https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009</a>.\n#\n# [2] Richard&nbsp;J. Gowers, Max Linke, Jonathan Barnoud, Tyler J.&nbsp;E. Reddy, Manuel&nbsp;N. Melo, Sean&nbsp;L. Seyler, Jan Doma\u0144ski, David&nbsp;L. Dotson, S\u00e9bastien Buchoux, Ian&nbsp;M. Denning, Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf, and Oliver Beckstein.\n# <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">MDAnalysis</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">A</span> toolkit for the analysis of molecular dynamics simulations.\n# <em>Journal of Computational Chemistry</em>, 32(10):2319\u20132327, July 2011.\n# 00778.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787\">http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">doi:10.1002/jcc.21787</a>.\n#\n# [4] Douglas&nbsp;L. Theobald.\n# Rapid calculation of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">RMSDs</span> using a quaternion-based characteristic polynomial.\n# <em>Acta Crystallographica Section A Foundations of Crystallography</em>, 61(4):478\u2013480, July 2005.\n# 00127.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266\">http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">doi:10.1107/S0108767305015266</a>.\n",

    "review": "## Private scientific scope, fidelity and verifiability assessment\n\n### Scientific endpoint inventory\nThe notebook's terminal scientific results, all keyed to the AdK closed\u2192open trajectory (98 frames, indices 0\u201397):\n\n1. **Universe-level backbone RMSD branch** (`R = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='backbone', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], ref_frame=0)`): Backbone/CORE/LID/NMP RMSD per frame.     "task_brief": "# RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed\u2192open transition\n\n## Background and objective\n\nYou are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value).** Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition, and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs.** Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using **all backbone atoms** (fitting group), minimizing the backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:\n\n1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;\n2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed **after that single backbone superposition only** \u2014 no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.\n\n**C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD.** Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using **only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain** as the fitting group, and report the RMSD of that group.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted branch.** Fitting group = **all protein alpha-carbons** (residue identifier 1\u2013214), with **mass weighting**. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. ---- D: mass-weighted branch ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    Rm = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\n    Rm.run()\n    a = Rm.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],\n                  'CORE': a[:, 3],\n                  'LID': a[:, 4],\n                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'mass_weighted_rmsd.csv'),\n                          index=False)\n\n    # ---- E: residue-number-weighted branch ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\n    core = u.select_atoms(CORE)\n    lid = u.select_atoms(LID)\n    nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n    Rr = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                  weights=ag.resids,\n                  weights_groupselections=[core.resids, lid.resids,\n                                           nmp.resids])\n    Rr.run()\n    a = Rr.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],\n                  'CORE': a[:, 3],\n                  'LID': a[:, 4],\n                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'resid_weighted_rmsd.csv'),\n                          index=False)\n\n    print('oracle complete: %s' % out)\n\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n",

These recovered values have not yet been independently validated and are flagged as pending validation here.\n\nMethodology fidelity facts preserved from the review: (a) the mass branch's groupselections are mass-weighted \u2014 MDAnalysis 2.11.0 RMSD.__init__ defaults weights_groupselections=False and _prepare then applies weights='mass' to all groupselections; the public question therefore defines D.2 as mass-weighted domain RMSDs (the notebook's \"remain unweighted\" narrative is recorded, not propagated); (b) groupselection semantics: one rigid transform per frame fit on the select group (weighted centroid matching plus optimal rotation applied to all atoms), domain RMSDs computed after that single superposition with no per-group re-alignment (the +ref_com translation is part of the transform) \u2014 stated explicitly in the public question; (c) reference-frame weight normalization (weights divided by their mean) is mathematically identical to sqrt(\u03a3w\u1d62d\u1d62\u00b2/\u03a3w\u1d62), so the public question uses the standard form; (d) interval endpoints for domains are the source's (LID 122\u2013159, NMP 30\u201359); (e) C restricts select=CORE to the 'name CA' AtomGroup, i.e. CORE alpha-carbons.\n\nOracle: uses only the supplied inputs; recomputes all five endpoints with the installed MDAnalysis 2.11.0 (the reference package), loading fresh universes per branch so branch A reads frame-0 positions before any iteration; no reference answers, hidden caches or author artifacts are accessed. Output schemas match the declared columns exactly (Frame as integer 0\u201397; single-row open-closed file with column Backbone).\n\nLeakage considerations: the oracle never touches the reference directory; recovered/projected reference values live only in the derivation destination; the public instruction contains no measured values.   "public_instruction": "# RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed\u2192open transition\n\n## Background and objective\n\nYou are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. AdK has three domains whose backbone positions move differently around a comparatively stable CORE:\n\n- **CORE**: residues 1\u201329, 60\u2013121, 160\u2013214\n- **LID**: residues 122\u2013159\n- **NMP**: residues 30\u201359\n\nAll domain selections below are applied to **backbone atoms**. Here \"backbone atoms\" means the N, CA, C and O atoms of the protein residues (the standard protein backbone selection); \"alpha-carbon\" means the atom named CA in each residue; residue identifiers (resid) are the topology's residue numbering, 1\u2013214.\n\nCompute the following root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) results, in **\u00c5ngstr\u00f6m**, over the full trajectory (frame indices 0\u201397; frame 0 is the closed-state starting structure):\n\n$$\\mathrm{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}^{ref})=\\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_i w_i\\,|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}^{ref}_i|^2}{\\sum_i w_i}}$$\n\nwith $w_i=1$ where no weighting is stated. \"Optimal rigid-body superposition\" means the translation and rotation minimizing the (weighted) RMSD of the stated fitting group; the translation places the fitting group's (weighted) centroid onto the reference's, followed by the optimal rotation. Where mass weighting is used, atomic masses are those given in the topology.\n\n## Inputs (read-only)\n\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk.psf` \u2014 topology (PSF format; 3341 atoms) for both the trajectory and the open-state structure.\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_dims.dcd` \u2014 trajectory sampling the closed\u2192open transition (98 frames).\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_open.crd` \u2014 open-state AdK coordinates (PDB 4AKE mapped onto this topology).\n\nThe trajectory and the open-state structure share the same topology, so selections produce atom sets in identical order.\n\n## Required analyses\n\n**A. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value).** Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition (unweighted), and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs.** Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using **all backbone atoms** (fitting group), minimizing the (unweighted) backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:\n\n1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;\n2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed **after that single backbone superposition only** \u2014 no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.\n\n**C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD.** Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using **only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain** as the fitting group, and report the (unweighted) RMSD of that group.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted branch.** Fitting group = **all protein alpha-carbons** (residues 1\u2013214), with **mass weighting**. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. Report, per frame:\n\n1. the mass-weighted alpha-carbon RMSD of the fitting group;\n2. the mass-weighted RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP \u2014 backbone atoms weighted by atomic mass), computed after the same single superposition, with no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering.\n\n**E. Residue-number-weighted branch.** Same fitting group and procedure as D, but the weight of every atom is its **residue number** (resid): the fitting-group alpha-carbon RMSD is resid-weighted, and each domain's RMSD is computed on its backbone atoms, each weighted by its residue number, after the same single superposition (no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering). This is an unconventional weighting used here to demonstrate custom-weight RMSD; it is part of the requested result.\n\nIn all trajectory analyses (B\u2013E) the reference is trajectory frame 0, and every frame of the trajectory (0\u201397) is analyzed.\n\n## Output files (CSV)\n\nWrite these files to the output directory. One row per trajectory frame (`Frame` = integer frame index 0\u202697), one row set per file. RMSD values in \u00c5. Only the columns listed below are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored.\n\n1. `backbone_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `Backbone`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis B).\n2. `ca_core_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `CORE` (analysis C).\n3. `mass_weighted_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `C-alphas`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis D).\n4. `resid_weighted_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `C-alphas`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis E).\n5. `open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv` \u2014 a single row with column `Backbone` (analysis A).\n\nAll values are finite; no missing values are expected.
