  "code": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed->open transition.\n\nStandalone implementation: topologies / coordinates are read with MDAnalysis\n(file parsing only); the RMSD and superposition mathematics is implemented\ndirectly from NumPy primitives (weighted Kabsch algorithm).\n\nUsage:  python solve.py --input-dir PATH --output-dir PATH\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport os\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- selections\n# Domain definitions (topology residue numbering 1-214), applied to backbone\n# atoms (N, CA, C, O) or alpha-carbons (CA) as stated per analysis.\nDOMAINS = {\n    \"CORE\": \"resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214\",\n    \"LID\": \"resid 122-159\",\n    \"NMP\": \"resid 30-59\",\n}\nDOMAIN_RESIDUES = {  # number of residues per domain\n    \"CORE\": (29 - 1 + 1) + (121 - 60 + 1) + (214 - 160 + 1),\n    \"LID\": 159 - 122 + 1,\n    \"NMP\": 59 - 30 + 1,\n}\n# expected number of backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O) per domain; residue 214 is\n# C-terminal (OT1/OT2 instead of O) so it contributes only N, CA, C.\nEXPECTED_DOMAIN_ATOMS = {\"CORE\": 583, \"LID\": 152, \"NMP\": 120}\n\n# possible subdirectories of the input directory holding the task files\nINPUT_SUBDIRS = (\"\", \"mdanalysis-rmsd\", \"inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd\")\n\n\ndef find_input(input_dir, filename):\n    \"\"\"Locate an input file directly in input_dir or in a task subdirectory.\"\"\"\n    for sub in INPUT_SUBDIRS:\n        path = os.path.join(input_dir, sub, filename)\n        if os.path.isfile(path):\n            return os.path.abspath(path)\n    raise FileNotFoundError(\n        f\"could not locate {filename!r} under {input_dir!r} \"\n        f\"(searched subdirectories: {INPUT_SUBDIRS})\"\n    )\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------- linear algebra\ndef weighted_kabsch(mobile, ref, weights=None):\n    \"\"\"Optimal (weighted) rigid-body superposition of `mobile` onto `ref`.\n\n    Returns (rotation R, translation t) such that the transformed mobile\n    coordinates are  mobile @ R.T + t  and the (weighted) RMSD of `mobile` onto\n    `ref` is minimal.  Weights default to 1 for every atom.\n\n    The translation first places the (weighted) centroid of `mobile` onto the\n    (weighted) centroid of `ref`; the optimal rotation is then obtained from the\n    SVD of the weighted covariance matrix (proper rotation, det(R) = +1).\n    \"\"\"\n    mobile = np.asarray(mobile, dtype=np.float64)\n    ref = np.asarray(ref, dtype=np.float64)\n    if weights is None:\n        weights = np.ones(mobile.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)\n    else:\n        weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.float64)\n\n    wsum = weights.sum()\n    cx = (weights[:, None] * mobile).sum(axis=0) / wsum\n    cy = (weights[:, None] * ref).sum(axis=0) / wsum\n\n    X = mobile - cx\n    Y = ref - cy\n\n    # H = sum_i w_i X_i Y_i^T  (rows of X, Y)\n    H = (X * weights[:, None]).T @ Y\n    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H)\n    d = np.sign(np.linalg.det(Vt.T @ U.T))\n    D = np.diag([1.0, 1.0, d])\n    R = Vt.T @ D @ U.T  # Y ~= (X @ R.T)\n    # translation: R(x - cx) + cy  ==  x @ R.T + (cy - cx @ R.T)\n    t = cy - cx @ R.T\n    return R, t\n\n\ndef transform(coords, R, t):\n    return np.asarray(coords, dtype=np.float64) @ R.T + t\n\n\ndef rmsd(a, b, weights=None):\n    \"\"\"RMSD = sqrt(sum_i w_i |a_i - b_i|^2 / sum_i w_i); w_i = 1 if None.\"\"\"\n    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64)\n    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=np.float64)\n    d2 = ((a - b) ** 2).sum(axis=1)\n    if weights is None:\n        return float(np.sqrt(d2.sum() / a.shape[0]))\n    weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.float64)\n    return float(np.sqrt((weights * d2).sum() / weights.sum()))\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------- helpers\ndef build_selections(universe):\n    \"\"\"Atom selections in topology order (identical order for trajectory and\n    open-state coordinates since both share the same topology).\"\"\"\n    backbone = universe.select_atoms(\"name N CA C O and protein\")\n    calpha = universe.select_atoms(\"name CA and protein\")\n\n    sel = {\n        \"backbone\": backbone,\n        \"calpha\": calpha,\n        \"domains_bb\": {},\n        \"domains_ca\": {},\n        \"resid_bb\": {},\n    }\n    for name, selstr in DOMAINS.items():\n        d_bb = backbone.select_atoms(selstr)\n        d_ca = calpha.select_atoms(selstr)\n        # one alpha-carbon per residue of the domain\n        assert d_ca.n_atoms == DOMAIN_RESIDUES[name], (name, d_ca.n_atoms)\n        # residue 214 is C-terminal (no O atom named O) -> -1 for that domain\n        expected = 4 * DOMAIN_RESIDUES[name] - (1 if name == \"CORE\" else 0)\n        assert d_bb.n_atoms == expected == EXPECTED_DOMAIN_ATOMS[name], name\n        sel[\"domains_bb\"][name] = d_bb\n        sel[\"domains_ca\"][name] = d_ca\n        sel[\"resid_bb\"][name] = d_bb.resids.astype(np.float64)\n    assert calpha.n_atoms == 214, calpha.n_atoms\n    assert backbone.n_atoms == 855, backbone.n_atoms\n    assert sum(DOMAIN_RESIDUES.values()) == 214\n    assert sum(EXPECTED_DOMAIN_ATOMS.values()) == 855\n    assert np.array_equal(backbone.indices, np.sort(backbone.indices))\n    assert np.array_equal(calpha.indices, np.sort(calpha.indices))\n    return sel\n\n\ndef frame_positions(universe, frame):\n    universe.trajectory[frame]\n    return universe.atoms.positions.astype(np.float64).copy()\n\n\n# ----------------------------------------------------------------- analyses\ndef analysis_A(traj_universe, open_universe, sel):\n    \"\"\"Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD after optimal unweighted superposition.\"\"\"\n    closed = frame_positions(traj_universe, 0)[sel[\"backbone\"].indices]\n    opened = open_universe.atoms.positions.astype(np.float64)[\n        sel[\"backbone\"].indices\n    ]\n    # center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry\n    closed = closed - closed.mean(axis=0)\n    opened = opened - opened.mean(axis=0)\n    # optimal unweighted rigid-body superposition\n    R, t = weighted_kabsch(closed, opened)\n    fitted = transform(closed, R, t)\n    return rmsd(fitted, opened)\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    ap.add_argument(\"--input-dir\", required=True)\n    ap.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", required=True)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    outd = args.output_dir\n    os.makedirs(outd, exist_ok=True)\n\n    psf = find_input(args.input_dir, \"adk.psf\")\n    dcd = find_input(args.input_dir, \"adk_dims.dcd\")\n    crd = find_input(args.input_dir, \"adk_open.crd\")\n\n    universe = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    open_universe = mda.Universe(psf, crd)\n    sel = build_selections(universe)\n    n_frames = universe.trajectory.n_frames\n\n    # reference = trajectory frame 0 (closed state)\n    ref_all = frame_positions(universe, 0)\n    ref_bb = ref_all[sel[\"backbone\"].indices]\n    ref_ca = ref_all[sel[\"calpha\"].indices]\n    ref_domain_bb = {k: ref_all[v.indices] for k, v in sel[\"domains_bb\"].items()}\n    ref_domain_ca = {k: ref_all[v.indices] for k, v in sel[\"domains_ca\"].items()}\n\n    ca_masses = sel[\"calpha\"].masses.astype(np.float64)\n    ca_resids = sel[\"calpha\"].resids.astype(np.float64)\n    domain_bb_masses = {\n        k: v.masses.astype(np.float64) for k, v in sel[\"domains_bb\"].items()\n    }\n    domain_bb_resids = sel[\"resid_bb\"]\n\n    rows_B, rows_C, rows_D, rows_E = [], [], [], []\n\n    for frame in range(n_frames):\n        positions = frame_positions(universe, frame)\n\n        # ------------- analysis B: fit on all backbone atoms (unweighted) ----\n        mob_bb = positions[sel[\"backbone\"].indices]\n        R, t = weighted_kabsch(mob_bb, ref_bb, None)\n        fitted = transform(positions, R, t)\n        r_dom = {\n            name: rmsd(fitted[d.indices], ref_domain_bb[name])\n            for name, d in sel[\"domains_bb\"].items()\n        }\n        rows_B.append({\n            \"Frame\": frame,\n            \"Backbone\": rmsd(fitted[sel[\"backbone\"].indices], ref_bb),\n            \"CORE\": r_dom[\"CORE\"],\n            \"LID\": r_dom[\"LID\"],\n            \"NMP\": r_dom[\"NMP\"],\n        })\n\n        # ------------- analysis C: fit on alpha-carbons of CORE --------------\n        core = sel[\"domains_ca\"][\"CORE\"]\n        mob_core = positions[core.indices]\n        R, t = weighted_kabsch(mob_core, ref_domain_ca[\"CORE\"], None)\n        fitted_core = transform(mob_core, R, t)\n        rows_C.append({\n            \"Frame\": frame,\n            \"CORE\": rmsd(fitted_core, ref_domain_ca[\"CORE\"]),\n        })\n\n        # --- analyses D (mass) and E (resid): fit on all alpha-carbons ------\n        mob_ca = positions[sel[\"calpha\"].indices]\n        for weights, rows, dom_w in (\n            (ca_masses, rows_D, domain_bb_masses),\n            (ca_resids, rows_E, domain_bb_resids),\n        ):\n            R, t = weighted_kabsch(mob_ca, ref_ca, weights)\n            fitted = transform(positions, R, t)\n            r_ca = rmsd(fitted[sel[\"calpha\"].indices], ref_ca, weights)\n            r_dom = {\n                name: rmsd(\n                    fitted[sel[\"domains_bb\"][name].indices],\n                    ref_domain_bb[name],\n                    dom_w[name],\n                )\n                for name in (\"CORE\", \"LID\", \"NMP\")\n            }\n            rows.append({\n                \"Frame\": frame,\n                \"C-alphas\": r_ca,\n                \"CORE\": r_dom[\"CORE\"],\n                \"LID\": r_dom[\"LID\"],\n                \"NMP\": r_dom[\"NMP\"],\n            })\n\n    # ---------------------------- analysis A -------------------------------\n    val_A = analysis_A(universe, open_universe, sel)\n    universe.trajectory.close()\n\n    def write_csv(rows, filename, columns):\n        pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=columns).to_csv(\n            os.path.join(outd, filename), index=False\n        )\n\n    write_csv(rows_B, \"backbone_rmsd.csv\",\n              [\"Frame\", \"Backbone\", \"CORE\", \"LID\", \"NMP\"])\n    write_csv(rows_C, \"ca_core_rmsd.csv\", [\"Frame\", \"CORE\"])\n    write_csv(rows_D, \"mass_weighted_rmsd.csv\",\n              [\"Frame\", \"C-alphas\", \"CORE\", \"LID\", \"NMP\"])\n    write_csv(rows_E, \"resid_weighted_rmsd.csv\",\n              [\"Frame\", \"C-alphas\", \"CORE\", \"LID\", \"NMP\"])\n    pd.DataFrame({\"Backbone\": [val_A]}).to_csv(\n        os.path.join(outd, \"open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv\"), index=False\n    )\n\n    print(\"A open-vs-closed backbone RMSD: {:.6f} A\".format(val_A))\n    print(\"frames analyzed:\", n_frames)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n",

B: fit on all backbone atoms (unweighted) then compute CORE/LID/NMP RMSD from the same single transform. C: fit and report on CORE alpha-carbons only. Prompt

Actual system prompt

autonomous-runs/063/explorer-evidence/grading/grader/system-prompt.md

Construct a scientific-content grader for the specified task

You are the GLM grading worker. Produce a public acceptance contract and a deterministic Python grader for the already specified task. Preserve its scientific question and selected outputs. Earlier notebook exports may include branches now excluded by the approved task policy; do not reinstate them. This stage evaluates saved outputs and available recomputations; it does not construct a Harbor image.

Inputs and tools

The user message contains the current task question, source/export evidence, task policy, measured repeatability results and available execution records. Use those executed records for validation facts; earlier planning proposals are not additional requirements or evidence that a check has run. When prior_worker_draft is supplied without a shell tool, finalize that existing work into a complete submission using the recorded observations and current question. Do not start another investigation. Local tests are evidence, not controller acceptance; failed or unfinished commands do not establish findings. Do not invent new measurements. Submit the full candidate promptly; the controller will execute its checks and return demonstrated defects for repair. It names the directory containing private reference output files in your sandbox. For each authoring or repair session, submit the candidate or repair response from the supplied task, schemas and execution evidence before using the shell. The controller resolves retained repair fields and runs the basic acceptance and rejection checks; do not duplicate them in exploratory scripts before submission. After a candidate attempt, shell access is available to diagnose its measured failures and repair the grader. If the evidence cannot support a candidate, return blocked with the reason. This ordering does not establish correctness: all later independent probes and review are still required. The shell tool, when supplied, runs offline with the reference's resolved Python packages. You can inspect those output files and installed package sources, and experiment in your writable working directory. You cannot modify the controller's reference copies. When paths supplies task inputs and recomputed outputs, inspect those as recorded evidence too. Otherwise raw biological inputs are not available. Do not rerun the entire analysis in this grader-author stage; independently executed controls are the evidence for recomputation agreement.

Use submit_artifact (or revise_artifact after rejection) to return the initial complete candidate: public instructions, grader code, named checks and rationale. A repair response may retain unchanged fields as described below. Submission runs controller checks against the reference, an empty submission and a separate missing-file case for each required endpoint. Rejections return actual evidence; repair the candidate, never the reference data or the target scientific methods. A separate worker will generate scientific counterexamples without seeing your grader. In a repair session, those frozen probes and measured failures are supplied.

In that existing repair session only, the response schema also permits probe_expectations: corrections to named probes' check_ids and rationale. Use this only when the review and public rules show an annotation is wrong, not to fit an observed grader result. A changed file need not violate all associated checks; an edit may preserve identities or cross-file relations. Do not change a correct grader to force an incorrect annotation to fail. Explain each correction from the unchanged public scientific requirement and mutation. Omit unaffected probes from this list. Every original script, name, kind, focus and source citation stays fixed, every wrong submission must still be rejected overall, and scientific check coverage cannot be removed. All basic controls and original mutation scripts run again against the repaired candidate. If a probe's script or intended overall acceptance is scientifically wrong, report a blocker; these annotations cannot repair that defect. Independent review sees both original and revised annotations.

The same repair response may also supply probe_concerns, a complete corrected list of suite-level concern annotations. Omit it or return null to preserve the original list. Correct stale descriptions from the actual script and recorded execution; do not remove a genuine scientific objection to obtain acceptance. This field cannot change mutations, intended outcomes or scientific coverage. Original concerns remain preserved alongside the effective list.

Public contract

Return only the acceptance-rule addendum in instruction; the controller retains and combines it with the approved scientific question. Do not replace the question with a function-by-function reference recipe. Resolve representational ambiguities without changing the scientific target. If the target itself is contradictory, report a blocker. Keep software choice open and distinguish demonstrated agreement from untested portability. Never disclose measured answer values or private hashes.

Specify exactly what is compared: files, identifiers, columns, row alignment and ordering, duplicates, missing values, nonfinite numbers, categorical identities, and numeric comparisons. Every acceptance rule must appear in the public text. For relative numeric tolerances, state the reference/denominator convention so the acceptance boundary is determined by the public rule. Explain cross-file consistency without confusing tables with different row units. Distinguish potentially missing annotations from mandatory identifiers/assignments.

Independently executed outputs are a comparison attempt, not a second oracle. Successful execution proves neither scientific correctness nor agreement with the public question. Diagnose disagreements against the stated task, source evidence and inspected data. Do not broaden acceptance or change entity identity merely to make that control pass. If the independent program or the public contract needs repair beyond this grader stage, return disposition: blocked with the specific reason. The controller cannot repair those scientific artifacts for you.

An equivalence rule must account for every accepted record and value. Retaining correct answers while appending unsupported values is not a valid alternative. Check coverage and multiplicity as well as membership; do not replace the requested output grain with a coarser set comparison to conceal a disagreement.

Use the measured repeatability evidence. Byte-identical reference runs do not make file hashes an appropriate grader or establish cross-stack portability. Compare parsed scientific content, retaining precision and identity. Establish any tolerance from a stated numerical/serialization argument and test its boundary; do not invent a generous threshold, round away meaningful errors, or copy a universal epsilon onto unrelated quantities. Exact comparison is permissible where justified and publicly stated. Reject nonfinite/invalid values explicitly; never let NaN make a numerical failure disappear. Preserve meaningful zero values. When a requested artifact can also be a normal hand-off between analysis steps, check whether a valid write/read round trip changes downstream numeric results. Matching implementations that share an in-memory precision path do not establish zero tolerance for that publicly allowed workflow. Use the independent execution evidence; report a specific gap if it does not exercise the relevant boundary. Normalize representation differences only when their consequences for every dependent endpoint are resolved and can be validated. Use stable identifiers for alignment; arbitrary row order is not a scientific target. Validate uniqueness, coverage and multiplicity before normalization. Do not require original row order or literal arbitrary labels merely because the reference used them. Do not add those equivalences just because they sound plausible. No independent software-equivalence claim can be established by modifying a copy of reference outputs. Use supplied independently executed outputs when establishing numerical rules. Do not mistake synthetic edits of answers for independent recomputation. If evidence is insufficient for a claimed tolerance or freedom, report the specific missing check rather than substituting an exact-recipe requirement.

Keep this stage focused: inspect the needed data properties, implement the comparator, and submit a complete candidate. Controller submission executes basic controls; a separate worker owns the independent mutation suite. Do not duplicate that suite or spend the session repeatedly auditing unrelated source internals.

Repair sessions

When a prior candidate and review are supplied, repair the identified defects in that candidate. Keep the supplied check definitions and frozen probes unchanged; report a blocker if a scientific change to either is necessary. The repair response schema contains only editable fields. Do not return or rephrase the check inventory: the controller carries its exact original definitions into the repaired artifact. You may inspect those definitions in prior_candidate when correcting the implementation; they remain the public acceptance requirements. Return null for instruction or grader_code when that field needs no change: the controller retains its exact prior text. For annotation-only corrections, retain both fields and return only the needed probe annotations and your rationale. When either field needs changes, return its complete replacement, not a diff. The resolved complete candidate still undergoes every frozen control and fresh review. A blocked response may retain those fields too; do not invent a grader stub to fill the response schema. Correct misleading explanations in the addendum or private rationale without changing the acceptance criteria. Describe numeric tolerances as limits on observable output differences, not as guarantees that every use of a particular wrong method will be detected. Keep run-specific calibration measurements and test history in the private rationale. Keep the rationale focused on the scientific comparison rules, their numerical justification, changes made and unresolved limitations. Do not recount control totals, maintain a test-history section, or declare the current passing/failing inventory: the controller owns those measured reports and will execute new tests after submission. You may cite specific feedback to explain why a correction is scientifically valid, without copying a mutable validation summary into prose. Check the complete revised candidate's claims, not just the paragraph named in review.

Submit this repair response before using the shell in this repair session. If that submission fails, use targeted diagnostics for the returned failures and resubmit the corrected candidate. The controller reruns all frozen controls on submission. Do not reconstruct their scripts, repeatedly run the entire suite locally, or expand into unrelated edge cases after the reported defects are resolved. Repeat a test only when a relevant code change, failed check, or unresolved review finding justifies it. Submission feedback is the next step; a local passing test is not final acceptance.

Grader interface

When authoring or replacing grader_code, return a complete Python program. An unchanged repair may return null as described above. The program accepts exactly:

python grade.py --reference-dir PATH --submission-dir PATH --report PATH

Reference and submission directories contain only the declared endpoint files. The supplied artifact_interface defines path resolution. Each output path is relative to each directory argument: read reference_dir / path and submission_dir / path. The submission argument already names the output root; in Harbor it is /workspace/outputs, not /workspace. A public instruction to write under outputs/ does not add another outputs/ below that root. Do not search fallback directories. The controller also tests correct values moved under an extra outputs/ layer; those files are at the wrong declared paths. Read reference values dynamically; do not embed answer arrays, expected dimensions, cluster counts or result hashes. Never import or execute submission code. Treat missing, malformed, duplicate, out-of-range and nonfinite data as failed checks, not successful runs or uncaught exceptions. Do not use paths, timestamps, environment variables or probe names to identify which control is running. Do not write to reference or submission files. Network access is unavailable.

Write this JSON object to --report, with no additional keys:

{"passed": true, "checks": [{"id": "check_id", "passed": true, "message": "..."}]}

Emit every declared check exactly once even for empty or malformed submissions. passed is the conjunction of all check booleans. Exit 0 after writing a valid report for either a correct or incorrect submission. A crash or timeout is an incomplete verification, not evidence of rejecting a wrong scientific result. Use only the installed packages and finish within the supplied verifier deadline.

Declare each check's unique id, kind (structural or scientific), covered artifact paths, and public requirement. Split distinct scientific results into meaningful named checks so controls can target them; do not hide an independent branch behind a superficial schema or file-existence check. Every required artifact must have scientific coverage, including scientifically meaningful metadata. Cross-file checks may cover several artifacts. Do not add arbitrary numbers of checks or unrelated requirements.

The rationale is private: justify comparison choices, cite source/serialization facts, distinguish evidence from assumptions, and state unresolved limitations. An accepted candidate still requires independent probes, review and later Harbor packaging validation. It does not yet constitute a released task.

If blocked, submit disposition: "blocked" and explain the evidence gap in the private rationale/concerns. Ready artifacts use disposition: "ready". A blocked submission stops this stage; do not fabricate a candidate just to fill the schema.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

    "code": "#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed->open transition.\n\nStandalone implementation: topologies / coordinates are read with MDAnalysis\n(file parsing only); the RMSD and superposition mathematics is implemented\ndirectly from NumPy primitives (weighted Kabsch algorithm).\n\nUsage:  python solve.py --input-dir PATH --output-dir PATH\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport os\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------- selections\n# Domain definitions (topology residue numbering 1-214), applied to backbone\n# atoms (N, CA, C, O) or alpha-carbons (CA) as stated per analysis.\nDOMAINS = {\n    \"CORE\": \"resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214\",\n    \"LID\": \"resid 122-159\",\n    \"NMP\": \"resid 30-59\",\n}\nDOMAIN_RESIDUES = {  # number of residues per domain\n    \"CORE\": (29 - 1 + 1) + (121 - 60 + 1) + (214 - 160 + 1),\n    \"LID\": 159 - 122 + 1,\n    \"NMP\": 59 - 30 + 1,\n}\n# expected number of backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O) per domain; residue 214 is\n# C-terminal (OT1/OT2 instead of O) so it contributes only N, CA, C.\nEXPECTED_DOMAIN_ATOMS = {\"CORE\": 583, \"LID\": 152, \"NMP\": 120}\n\n# possible subdirectories of the input directory holding the task files\nINPUT_SUBDIRS = (\"\", \"mdanalysis-rmsd\", \"inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd\")\n\n\ndef find_input(input_dir, filename):\n    \"\"\"Locate an input file directly in input_dir or in a task subdirectory.\"\"\"\n    for sub in INPUT_SUBDIRS:\n        path = os.path.join(input_dir, sub, filename)\n        if os.path.isfile(path):\n            return os.path.abspath(path)\n    raise FileNotFoundError(\n        f\"could not locate {filename!r} under {input_dir!r} \"\n        f\"(searched subdirectories: {INPUT_SUBDIRS})\"\n    )\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------- linear algebra\ndef weighted_kabsch(mobile, ref, weights=None):\n    \"\"\"Optimal (weighted) rigid-body superposition of `mobile` onto `ref`.\n\n    Returns (rotation R, translation t) such that the transformed mobile\n    coordinates are  mobile @ R.T + t  and the (weighted) RMSD of `mobile` onto\n    `ref` is minimal.  Weights default to 1 for every atom.\n\n    The translation first places the (weighted) centroid of `mobile` onto the\n    (weighted) centroid of `ref`; the optimal rotation is then obtained from the\n    SVD of the weighted covariance matrix (proper rotation, det(R) = +1).\n    \"\"\"\n    mobile = np.asarray(mobile, dtype=np.float64)\n    ref = np.asarray(ref, dtype=np.float64)\n    if weights is None:\n        weights = np.ones(mobile.shape[0], dtype=np.float64)\n    else:\n        weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.float64)\n\n    wsum = weights.sum()\n    cx = (weights[:, None] * mobile).sum(axis=0) / wsum\n    cy = (weights[:, None] * ref).sum(axis=0) / wsum\n\n    X = mobile - cx\n    Y = ref - cy\n\n    # H = sum_i w_i X_i Y_i^T  (rows of X, Y)\n    H = (X * weights[:, None]).T @ Y\n    U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H)\n    d = np.sign(np.linalg.det(Vt.T @ U.T))\n    D = np.diag([1.0, 1.0, d])\n    R = Vt.T @ D @ U.T  # Y ~= (X @ R.T)\n    # translation: R(x - cx) + cy  ==  x @ R.T + (cy - cx @ R.T)\n    t = cy - cx @ R.T\n    return R, t\n\n\ndef transform(coords, R, t):\n    return np.asarray(coords, dtype=np.float64) @ R.T + t\n\n\ndef rmsd(a, b, weights=None):\n    \"\"\"RMSD = sqrt(sum_i w_i |a_i - b_i|^2 / sum_i w_i); w_i = 1 if None.\"\"\"\n    a = np.asarray(a, dtype=np.float64)\n    b = np.asarray(b, dtype=np.float64)\n    d2 = ((a - b) ** 2).sum(axis=1)\n    if weights is None:\n        return float(np.sqrt(d2.sum() / a.shape[0]))\n    weights = np.asarray(weights, dtype=np.float64)\n    return float(np.sqrt((weights * d2).sum() / weights.sum()))\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------- helpers\ndef build_selections(universe):\n    \"\"\"Atom selections in topology order (identical order for trajectory and\n    open-state coordinates since both share the same topology).\"\"\"\n    backbone = universe.select_atoms(\"name N CA C O and protein\")\n    calpha = universe.select_atoms(\"name CA and protein\")\n\n    sel = {\n        \"backbone\": backbone,\n        \"calpha\": calpha,\n        \"domains_bb\": {},\n        \"domains_ca\": {},\n        \"resid_bb\": {},\n    }\n    for name, selstr in DOMAINS.items():\n        d_bb = backbone.select_atoms(selstr)\n        d_ca = calpha.select_atoms(selstr)\n        #       "oracle_code": "#!/usr/bin/env python\n\"\"\"Reference solution: AdK closed->open RMSD analyses A-E.\n\nUses only the supplied inputs under --input-dir; writes the five required\nCSVs to --output-dir.\n\"\"\"\nimport argparse\nimport os\n\nimport pandas as pd\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    ap.add_argument('--input-dir', required=True)\n    ap.add_argument('--output-dir', required=True)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    base = os.path.join(args.input_dir, 'mdanalysis-rmsd')\n    psf = os.path.join(base, 'adk.psf')\n    dcd = os.path.join(base, 'adk_dims.dcd')\n    crd = os.path.join(base, 'adk_open.crd')\n    out = args.output_dir\n    os.makedirs(out, exist_ok=True)\n\n    # ---- A: open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value) ----\n    # Trajectory universe freshly loaded, positioned at frame 0.\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    ref = mda.Universe(psf, crd)\n    oc = rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,\n                  ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,\n                  center=True, superposition=True)\n    pd.DataFrame({'Backbone': [float(oc)]}).to_csv(\n        os.path.join(out, 'open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv'), index=False)\n\n    # ---- B: backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    R = rms.RMSD(u, u, select='backbone',\n                 groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], ref_frame=0)\n    R.run()\n    a = R.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'Backbone': a[:, 2],\n                  'CORE': a[:, 3],\n                  'LID': a[:, 4],\n                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'backbone_rmsd.csv'), index=False)\n\n    # ---- C: alpha-carbon CORE RMSD ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    ca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n    R = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\n    R.run()\n    a = R.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'CORE': a[:, 2]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'ca_core_rmsd.csv'), index=False)\n\n    # ---- D: mass-weighted branch ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    Rm = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\n    Rm.run()\n    a = Rm.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],\n                  'CORE': a[:, 3],\n                  'LID': a[:, 4],\n                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'mass_weighted_rmsd.csv'),\n                          index=False)\n\n    # ---- E: residue-number-weighted branch ----\n    u = mda.Universe(psf, dcd)\n    ag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\n    core = u.select_atoms(CORE)\n    lid = u.select_atoms(LID)\n    nmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n    Rr = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                  weights=ag.resids,\n                  weights_groupselections=[core.resids, lid.resids,\n                                           nmp.resids])\n    Rr.run()\n    a = Rr.results.rmsd\n    pd.DataFrame({'Frame': a[:, 0].astype(int),\n                  'C-alphas': a[:, 2],\n                  'CORE': a[:, 3],\n                  'LID': a[:, 4],\n                  'NMP': a[:, 5]}\n                 ).to_csv(os.path.join(out, 'resid_weighted_rmsd.csv'),\n                          index=False)\n\n    print('oracle complete: %s' % out)\n\n\nif __name__ == '__main__':\n    main()\n",
      "output_paths": [
        "backbone_rmsd.csv",
        "ca_core_rmsd.csv",
        "mass_weighted_rmsd.csv",
        "resid_weighted_rmsd.csv",
        "open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv"
      ],
      "rationale": "Scope: the public task asks for the notebook's five terminal AdK RMSD endpoints (A open-vs-closed backbone value; B backbone-referenced trajectory branch with CORE/LID/NMP group selections; C CORE alpha-carbon branch; D mass-weighted branch; E resid-weighted branch), all over all 98 frames with frame 0 as trajectory reference. Endpoints B and A are not in the recorded exports (R and df overwritten / value never assigned); per the task_policy `endpoint_recovery` they are included by faithful recomputation of the unchanged original source calls on the same original inputs and required state, rather than being silently dropped. The derived artifact inventory is exactly the declared inputs plus the five reference CSVs; no extra files (e.g. provenance manifests) are written, so lineage is documented here.\n\nInput derivation: the three MDAnalysisTests data files (adk.psf, adk_dims.dcd, adk_open.crd) are copied byte-for-byte into destination/inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/ and verified against the recorded SHA-256 identities (96cec916\u2026, 859a5bd9\u2026, cd7f5e20\u2026). No transformation of the molecular data occurs; the public population is exactly the recorded one (3341 atoms, 98 frames, single chain, resid 1\u2013214), so there is no row/entity multiplicity question; the only group key is Frame per output row.\n\nReference projection: ca_core_rmsd.csv, mass_weighted_rmsd.csv and resid_weighted_rmsd.csv are projected from the recorded reference exports (byte-identical across 2 recorded replays); only the publicly compared columns are retained. The DCD-reader-guessed \"Time (ns)\" column is metadata (1-indexed frame-derived values \u2248 frame+1, unit label unverified), not a computed scientific quantity, so dropping it is an explicit projection, not a dropped branch. Values are unchanged.\n\nEndpoint recovery lineage (original reference artifacts untouched; recoveries written only under the new destination): (1) reference/backbone_rmsd.csv reruns the exact notebook call rms.RMSD(u, u, select='backbone', groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP], ref_frame=0).run() on a fresh Universe(psf, dcd) of the staged byte-identical adk.psf + adk_dims.dcd \u2014 each run() iteration re-reads frames from the DCD, so no in-memory position state is required and the run is independent of earlier notebook branches; (2) reference/open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv reruns the exact standalone rms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions, ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions, center=True, superposition=True) with u freshly loaded so the trajectory is positioned at frame 0 before positions are read (this call executed before any trajectory iteration in the notebook), using adk.psf + adk_dims.dcd + adk_open.crd. Both recoveries run in the pinned offline environment (MDAnalysis 2.11.0, the installed reference package). These recovered values have not yet been independently validated and are flagged as pending validation here.\n\nMethodology fidelity facts preserved from the review: (a) the mass branch's groupselections are mass-weighted \u2014 MDAnalysis 2.11.0 RMSD.__init__ defaults weights_groupselections=False and _prepare then applies weights='mass' to all groupselections; the public question therefore defines D.2 as mass-weighted domain RMSDs (the notebook's \"remain unweighted\" narrative is recorded, not propagated); (b) groupselection semantics: one rigid transform per frame fit on the select group (weighted centroid matching plus optimal rotation applied to all atoms), domain RMSDs computed after that single superposition with no per-group re-alignment (the +ref_com translation is part of the transform) \u2014 stated explicitly in the public question; (c) reference-frame weight normalization (weights divided by their mean) is mathematically identical to sqrt(\u03a3w\u1d62d\u1d62\u00b2/\u03a3w\u1d62), so the public question uses the standard form; (d) interval endpoints for domains are the source's (LID 122\u2013159, NMP 30\u201359); (e) C restricts select=CORE to the 'name CA' AtomGroup, i.e. CORE alpha-carbons.\n\nOracle: uses only the supplied inputs; recomputes all five endpoints with the installed MDAnalysis 2.11.0 (the reference package), loading fresh universes per branch so branch A reads frame-0 positions before any iteration; no reference answers, hidden caches or author artifacts are accessed. Output schemas match the declared columns exactly (Frame as integer 0\u201397; single-row open-closed file with column Backbone).\n\nLeakage considerations: the oracle never touches the reference directory; recovered/projected reference values live only in the derivation destination; the public instruction contains no measured values. Frame-0 self-comparison values are ~1e-7\u20131e-8 \u00c5, so numerical comparison will need an absolute floor component.\n\nRemaining comparison-stage questions (not resolved here): tolerance calibration (Kabsch vs QCP, float64; near-zero frame-0 absolute floor), independent implementation of the public contract, and administrative input-redistribution clearance for the LGPL-2.1 MDAnalysisTests data files. Pipeline status: task constructed from supplied source and recorded observations; reference branches 1\u20132 recovered per endpoint_recovery policy and pending independent validation."

  "source_evidence": {
    "candidate/pyproject.toml": "[project]\nname = \"mdanalysis-rmsd-setup\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.13\"\ndependencies = [\n    \"MDAnalysis==2.11.0\",\n    \"MDAnalysisTests==2.11.0\",\n    \"matplotlib==3.11.2\",\n    \"pandas==3.1.0\",\n]\n",
    "inputs/exports.py": "import os as _os\n\n_export_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\n_os.makedirs(_export_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\ndf.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"ca_core_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_mass.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"mass_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)\ndf_charge.to_csv(_os.path.join(_export_dir, \"resid_weighted_rmsd.csv\"), index=False)",
    "inputs/original.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: guide\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Calculating the root mean square deviation of atomic structures\n#\n# We calculate the RMSD of domains in adenylate kinase as it transitions from an open to closed structure, and look at calculating weighted RMSDs.\n#\n# **Last updated:** December 2022 with MDAnalysis 2.4.0-dev0\n#\n# **Minimum version of MDAnalysis:** 1.0.0\n#\n# **Packages required:**\n#     \n# * MDAnalysis (<a data-cite=\"michaud-agrawal_mdanalysis_2011\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">Michaud-Agrawal *et al.*, 2011</a>, <a data-cite=\"gowers_mdanalysis_2016\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.25080/Majora-629e541a-00e\">Gowers *et al.*, 2016</a>)\n# * MDAnalysisTests\n# * [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org)\n#\n# **See also**\n#\n# * [Pairwise (2D) RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb)\n# * [RMSF](rmsf.ipynb)\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# MDAnalysis implements RMSD calculation using the fast QCP algorithm (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>). Please cite (<a data-cite=\"theobald_rapid_2005\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">Theobald, 2005</a>) when using the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.align`` module in published work.\n#\n# </div>\n\nimport MDAnalysis as mda\nfrom MDAnalysis.tests.datafiles import PSF, DCD, CRD\nfrom MDAnalysis.analysis import rms\n\nimport pandas as pd\n# the next line is necessary to display plots in Jupyter\n# Notebook presentation directive: %matplotlib inline\n\n\n# ## Loading files\n\n# The test files we will be working with here feature adenylate kinase (AdK), a phosophotransferase enzyme. (<a data-cite=\"beckstein_zipping_2009\" href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">Beckstein *et al.*, 2009</a>) The trajectory ``DCD`` samples a transition from a closed to an open conformation. AdK has three domains: \n#\n#   * CORE\n#   * LID: an ATP-binding domain\n#   * NMP: an AMP-binding domain\n#   \n# The LID and NMP domains move around the stable CORE as the enzyme transitions between the opened and closed conformations. One way to quantify this movement is by calculating the root mean square deviation (RMSD) of atomic positions.\n\nu = mda.Universe(PSF, DCD)  # closed AdK (PDB ID: 1AKE)\nref = mda.Universe(PSF, CRD)  # open AdK (PDB ID: 4AKE)\n\n# ## Background\n#\n# The root mean square deviation (RMSD) of particle coordinates is one measure of distance, or dissimilarity, between molecular conformations. Each structure should have matching elementwise atoms $i$ in the same order, as the distance between them is calculated and summed for the final result. It is calculated between coordinate arrays $\\mathbf{x}$ and $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ according to the equation below:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{n} \\sum_{i=1}^{n}{|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}} $$\n#\n# As molecules can move around, the structure $\\mathbf{x}$ is usually translated by a vector $\\mathbf{t}$ and rotated by a matrix $\\mathsf{R}$ to align with the reference $\\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}$ such that the RMSD is minimised. The RMSD after this optimal superposition can be expressed as follows:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^{\\text{ref}}) = \\min_{\\mathsf{R}, \\mathbf{t}} %\n#   \\sqrt{\\frac{1}{N} \\sum_{i=1}^{N} \\left[ %\n#       (\\mathsf{R}\\cdot\\mathbf{x}_{i}(t) + \\mathbf{t}) - \\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\\text{ref}} \\right]^{2}}$$\n#\n# The RMSD between one reference state and a trajectory of structures is often calculated as a way to measure the dissimilarity of the trajectory conformational ensemble to the reference. This reference is frequently the first frame of the trajectory (the default in MDAnalysis), in which case it can provide insight into the overall movement from the initial starting point. While stable RMSD values from a reference structure are frequently used as a measure of conformational convergence, this metric suffers from the problem of *degeneracy*: many different structures can have the same RMSD from the same reference. For an alternative measure, you could use [pairwise or 2D RMSD](pairwise_rmsd.ipynb).\n#\n# Typically not all coordinates in a structures are included in an RMSD analysis. With proteins, the fluctuation of the residue side-chains is not representative of overall conformational change. Therefore when RMSD analyses are performed to investigate large-scale movements in proteins, the atoms are usually restricted only to the backbone atoms (forming the amide-bond chain) or the alpha-carbon atoms. \n#\n# MDAnalysis provides functions and classes to calculate the [RMSD between coordinate arrays](#RMSD-between-two-sets-of-coordinates), and [Universes](#RMSD-of-a-Universe-with-multiple-selections) or [AtomGroups](#RMSD-of-an-AtomGroup-with-multiple-selections). \n#\n# The contribution of each particle $i$ to the final RMSD value can also [be weighted](#Weighted-RMSD-of-a-trajectory) by $w_i$:\n#\n# $$ \\text{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x}, \\mathbf{x}^\\text{ref}) = \\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^{n}{w_i|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}_i^{\\text{ref}}|^2}}{\\sum_{i-1}^n w_i}} $$\n#\n# RMSD analyses are frequently weighted by mass. The MDAnalysis RMSD class ([API docs](https://docs.mdanalysis.org/stable/documentation_pages/analysis/rms.html#MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD)) allows you to both [select mass-weighting](#Mass) with `weights='mass'` or `weights_groupselections='mass'`, or to [pass custom arrays](#Custom-weights) into either keyword.\n\n# ## RMSD between two sets of coordinates\n\n# The ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function returns the root mean square deviation (in Angstrom) between two sets of coordinates. Here, we calculate the RMSD between the backbone atoms of the open and closed conformations of AdK. Only considering the backbone atoms is often more helpful than calculating the RMSD for all the atoms, as movement in amino acid side-chains isn't indicative of overall conformational change.\n\nrms.rmsd(u.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # coordinates to align\n         ref.select_atoms('backbone').positions,  # reference coordinates\n         center=True,  # subtract the center of geometry\n         superposition=True)  # superimpose coordinates\n\n# ## RMSD of a Universe with multiple selections\n\n# It is more efficient to use the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.RMSD`` class to calculate the RMSD of an entire trajectory to a single reference point, than to use the the ``MDAnalysis.analysis.rms.rmsd`` function.\n#\n# The ``rms.RMSD`` class first performs a rotational and translational alignment of the target trajectory to the reference universe at ``ref_frame``, using the atoms in ``select`` to determine the transformation. The RMSD of the ``select`` selection is calculated. Then, *without further alignment*, the RMSD of each group in ``groupselections`` is calculated. \n\nCORE = 'backbone and (resid 1-29 or resid 60-121 or resid 160-214)'\nLID = 'backbone and resid 122-159'\nNMP = 'backbone and resid 30-59'\n\nR = rms.RMSD(u,  # universe to align\n             u,  # reference universe or atomgroup\n             select='backbone',  # group to superimpose and calculate RMSD\n             groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],  # groups for RMSD\n             ref_frame=0)  # frame index of the reference\nR.run()\n\n# The data is saved in ``R.rmsd`` as an array.\n\nR.results.rmsd.shape\n\n# ``R.rmsd`` has a row for each timestep. The first two columns of each row are the frame index of the time step, and the time (which is guessed in trajectory formats without timesteps). The third column is RMSD of ``select``. The last few columns are the RMSD of the groups in ``groupselections``.\n\n# ### Plotting the data\n#\n# We can easily plot this data using the common data analysis package [pandas](https://pandas.pydata.org). We turn the ``R.rmsd`` array into a [DataFrame](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/dsintro.html#dataframe) and label each column below.\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'Backbone', 'CORE', \n                           'LID', 'NMP'])\n\ndf\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y=['Backbone', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'],\n             kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel(r'RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## RMSD of an AtomGroup with multiple selections\n#\n# The `RMSD` class accepts both `AtomGroup`s and `Universe`s as arguments. Restricting the atoms considered to an AtomGroup can be very helpful, as the `select` and `groupselections` arguments are applied only to the atoms in the original `AtomGroup`. In the example below, for example, only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain are incorporated in the analysis.\n#\n# <div class=\"alert alert-info\">\n#     \n# **Note**\n#\n# This feature does not currently support `groupselections`.\n#\n# </div>\n\nca = u.select_atoms('name CA')\n\nR = rms.RMSD(ca, ca, select=CORE, ref_frame=0)\nR.run()\n\ndf = pd.DataFrame(R.results.rmsd, \n                  columns=['Frame', 'Time (ns)', \n                           'CORE'])\n\nax = df.plot(x='Frame', y='CORE', kind='line')\nax.set_ylabel('RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## Weighted RMSD of a trajectory\n#\n# You can also calculate the weighted RMSD of a trajectory using the `weights` and `weights_groupselections` keywords. The former only applies weights to the group in `select`, while the latter must be a list of the *same length and order* as `groupselections`. If you would like to only weight certain groups in `groupselections`, use `None` for the unweighted groups. Both `weights` and `weights_groupselections` accept `None` (for unweighted), `'mass'` (to weight by mass), and custom arrays. A custom array should have the same number of values as there are particles in the corresponding AtomGroup.\n\n# ### Mass\n\n# It is common to weight RMSD analyses by particle weight, so the `RMSD` class accepts `'mass'` as an argument for `weights`. Note that the `weights` keyword only applies to the group in `select`, and does not apply to the `groupselections`; these remain unweighted below.\n\nR_mass = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                  select='protein and name CA',\n                  weights='mass',\n                  groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP])\nR_mass.run()\n\n# The plot looks largely the same as above because all the alpha-carbons and individual backbone atoms have the same mass. Below we show how you can pass in custom weights.\n\ndf_mass = pd.DataFrame(R_mass.results.rmsd, \n                       columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass = df_mass.plot(x='Frame', \n                       y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_mass.set_ylabel('Mass-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ### Custom weights\n\n# You can also pass in an array of values for the weights. This must have the same length as the number of atoms in your selection groups. In this example, we pass in arrays of residue numbers. This **is not a typical weighting you might choose**, but we use it here to show how you can get different results to the previous graphs for mass-weighted and non-weighted RMSD. You could choose to pass in an array of charges, or your own custom value. \n#\n# First we select the atom groups to make this easier.\n\nag = u.select_atoms('protein and name CA')\nprint('Shape of C-alpha charges:', ag.charges.shape)\ncore = u.select_atoms(CORE)\nlid = u.select_atoms(LID)\nnmp = u.select_atoms(NMP)\n\n# Below, we pass in weights for `ag` with the `weights` keyword, and weights for the `groupselections` with the `weights_groupselections` keyword.\n\nR_charge = rms.RMSD(u, u,\n                    select='protein and name CA',\n                    groupselections=[CORE, LID, NMP],\n                    weights=ag.resids,\n                    weights_groupselections=[core.resids, \n                                             lid.resids, \n                                             nmp.resids])\nR_charge.run()\n\n# You can see in the below graph that the NMP domain has much higher RMSD than before, as each particle is weighted by its residue number. Conversely, the CORE domain doesn't really change much. We could potentially infer from this that residues later in the NMP domain (with a higher residue number) are mobile during the length of the trajectory, whereas residues later in the CORE domain do not seem to contribute significantly to the RMSD.\n#\n# However, again, this is a **very non-conventional metric** and is shown here simply to demonstrate how to use the code.\n\ndf_charge = pd.DataFrame(R_charge.results.rmsd, \n                         columns=['Frame', \n                                'Time (ns)', \n                                'C-alphas', 'CORE', \n                                'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge = df_charge.plot(x='Frame',\n                           y=['C-alphas', 'CORE', 'LID', 'NMP'])\nax_charge.set_ylabel('Charge-weighted RMSD ($\\AA$)')\n\n# ## References\n#\n# [1] Oliver Beckstein, Elizabeth&nbsp;J. Denning, Juan&nbsp;R. Perilla, and Thomas&nbsp;B. Woolf.\n# Zipping and <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Unzipping</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Adenylate</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Kinase</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Atomistic</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Insights</span> into the <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Ensemble</span> of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Open</span>\u2194<span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Closed</span> <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">Transitions</span>.\n# <em>Journal of Molecular Biology</em>, 394(1):160\u2013176, November 2009.\n# 00107.\n# URL: <a href=\"https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164\">https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0022283609011164</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009\">doi:10.1016/j.jmb.2009.09.009</a>.\n#\n# [2] Richard&nbsp;J. Woolf, and Oliver Beckstein.\n# <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">MDAnalysis</span>: <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">A</span> toolkit for the analysis of molecular dynamics simulations.\n# <em>Journal of Computational Chemistry</em>, 32(10):2319\u20132327, July 2011.\n# 00778.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787\">http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/jcc.21787</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.21787\">doi:10.1002/jcc.21787</a>.\n#\n# [4] Douglas&nbsp;L. Theobald.\n# Rapid calculation of <span class=\"bibtex-protected\">RMSDs</span> using a quaternion-based characteristic polynomial.\n# <em>Acta Crystallographica Section A Foundations of Crystallography</em>, 61(4):478\u2013480, July 2005.\n# 00127.\n# URL: <a href=\"http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266\">http://scripts.iucr.org/cgi-bin/paper?S0108767305015266</a>, <a href=\"https://doi.org/10.1107/S0108767305015266\">doi:10.1107/S0108767305015266</a>.\n",

    "task_brief": "# RMSD analysis of the adenylate kinase closed\u2192open transition\n\n## Background and objective\n\nYou are given an atomistic molecular-dynamics trajectory of adenylate kinase (AdK) sampling the transition from a closed (PDB 1AKE) to an open (PDB 4AKE) conformation, a matching molecular topology, and an open-state reference coordinate file. AdK has three domains whose backbone positions move differently around a comparatively stable CORE:\n\n- **CORE**: residues 1\u201329, 60\u2013121, 160\u2013214\n- **LID**: residues 122\u2013159\n- **NMP**: residues 30\u201359\n\nAll domain selections below are applied to **backbone atoms**. Here \"backbone atoms\" means the N, CA, C and O atoms of the protein residues (the standard protein backbone selection); \"alpha-carbon\" means the atom named CA in each residue; residue identifiers (resid) are the topology's residue numbering, 1\u2013214.\n\nCompute the following root-mean-square-deviation (RMSD) results, in **\u00c5ngstr\u00f6m**, over the full trajectory (frame indices 0\u201397; frame 0 is the closed-state starting structure):\n\n$$\\mathrm{RMSD}(\\mathbf{x},\\mathbf{x}^{ref})=\\sqrt{\\frac{\\sum_i w_i\\,|\\mathbf{x}_i-\\mathbf{x}^{ref}_i|^2}{\\sum_i w_i}}$$\n\nwith $w_i=1$ where no weighting is stated. \"Optimal rigid-body superposition\" means the translation and rotation minimizing the (weighted) RMSD of the stated fitting group; the translation places the fitting group's (weighted) centroid onto the reference's, followed by the optimal rotation. Where mass weighting is used, atomic masses are those given in the topology.\n\n## Inputs (read-only)\n\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk.psf` \u2014 topology (PSF format; 3341 atoms) for both the trajectory and the open-state structure.\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_dims.dcd` \u2014 trajectory sampling the closed\u2192open transition (98 frames).\n- `inputs/mdanalysis-rmsd/adk_open.crd` \u2014 open-state AdK coordinates (PDB 4AKE mapped onto this topology).\n\nThe trajectory and the open-state structure share the same topology, so selections produce atom sets in identical order.\n\n## Required analyses\n\n**A. Open-vs-closed backbone RMSD (single value).** Take the backbone atoms of trajectory frame 0 (closed state) and of the open-state coordinates. Center both coordinate sets at their centers of geometry, apply optimal rigid-body superposition (unweighted), and report the resulting backbone RMSD.\n\n**B. Backbone-referenced trajectory RMSDs.** Use trajectory frame 0 as the reference. For each trajectory frame, superimpose the frame onto the reference using **all backbone atoms** (fitting group), minimizing the (unweighted) backbone RMSD. Report, per frame:\n\n1. the RMSD of the backbone fitting group itself;\n2. the RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP), computed **after that single backbone superposition only** \u2014 no per-domain re-alignment and no per-domain re-centering; the domain coordinates are simply the correspondingly transformed trajectory positions compared against the domain's reference (frame-0) positions.\n\n**C. Alpha-carbon CORE RMSD.** Restrict the analysis to the protein's alpha-carbon atoms. Superimpose each frame onto frame 0 using **only the alpha-carbons of the CORE domain** as the fitting group, and report the (unweighted) RMSD of that group.\n\n**D. Mass-weighted branch.** Fitting group = **all protein alpha-carbons** (residues 1\u2013214), with **mass weighting**. For each frame, superimpose onto frame 0 minimizing this weighted alpha-carbon RMSD. Report, per frame:\n\n1. the mass-weighted alpha-carbon RMSD of the fitting group;\n2. the mass-weighted RMSD of each domain selection (CORE, LID, NMP \u2014 backbone atoms weighted by atomic mass), computed after the same single superposition, with no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering.\n\n**E. Residue-number-weighted branch.** Same fitting group and procedure as D, but the weight of every atom is its **residue number** (resid): the fitting-group alpha-carbon RMSD is resid-weighted, and each domain's RMSD is computed on its backbone atoms, each weighted by its residue number, after the same single superposition (no per-domain re-alignment or re-centering). This is an unconventional weighting used here to demonstrate custom-weight RMSD; it is part of the requested result.\n\nIn all trajectory analyses (B\u2013E) the reference is trajectory frame 0, and every frame of the trajectory (0\u201397) is analyzed.\n\n## Output files (CSV)\n\nWrite these files to the output directory. One row per trajectory frame (`Frame` = integer frame index 0\u202697), one row set per file. RMSD values in \u00c5. Only the columns listed below are compared; any additional columns (such as a trajectory-derived time column) are ignored.\n\n1. `backbone_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `Backbone`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis B).\n2. `ca_core_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `CORE` (analysis C).\n3. `mass_weighted_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `C-alphas`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis D).\n4. `resid_weighted_rmsd.csv` \u2014 columns: `Frame`, `C-alphas`, `CORE`, `LID`, `NMP` (analysis E).\n5. `open_closed_backbone_rmsd.csv` \u2014 a single row with column `Backbone` (analysis A).\n\nAll values are finite; no missing values are expected. Rows are identified by `Frame`, and the frame keys must be identical across files 1\u20134.\n\n## Environment and constraints\n\nAny software may be used (an offline environment containing MDAnalysis 2.11.0 is available for convenience; its use is not required). Execution is offline. Limits: \u22644 CPU, \u22648 GiB RAM, \u226410 GiB disk, 600 s runtime."

GLM-5.3 · native high requested

09 · Challenge the grader

Author and execute meaningful wrong results and valid representation alternatives against the declared scientific checks.

Program: grading_session.py

Prompt

Actual system prompt

autonomous-runs/063/explorer-evidence/grading/probes/system-prompt.md

Independently challenge the public artifact acceptance contract

You are a separate GLM validation worker. You receive the public instructions, named check requirements, output paths, and private reference artifacts. You do not receive the grader implementation, analysis programs, or raw biological inputs. Inspect the reference result files with the offline shell tool as needed. Produce probes that test the stated scientific contract; do not assume the implementation is correct.

Build a compact suite and submit it once it covers the named requirements. Inspect only concrete facts needed to choose mutations. Do not re-derive the scientific workflow or duplicate a grader implementation. Select records from the existing result files and change their saved values or representation. Do not search the filesystem for analysis scripts or attempt to reconstruct raw inputs.

Batch related inspections. Once you have evidence for a mutation, write its script and move on rather than repeatedly checking the same records. Prefer deterministic selection from the copied output using explicit predicates and assertions over manually transcribing complete records into scripts. Save observations and scripts in the working directory so they can be reused. Submit when the required coverage is present: the controller already executes every script on a fresh copy. If preflight finds a defect, use its recorded failure to correct that defect; do not restart discovery or repeat successful checks without new evidence.

Return a suite using the supplied schema. Each probe has a stable name, kind (wrong_solution or valid_alternative), focus, rationale, source citations, Python script, and check_ids identifying its intended checks. Cover every scientific check with at least one meaningful wrong-result probe. A probe may cover several related checks only when it actually changes each corresponding result. Include valid representation controls for the freedoms the public contract permits. Test numerical tolerance boundaries and nonfinite inputs where applicable. Identify ambiguity or an unjustified acceptance rule in concerns.

When a claimed equivalence permits multiple records or values for one entity, challenge it by retaining correct answers and adding a plausible but unsupported value, not only by inserting exact duplicates. Every accepted addition must have a justification that can actually be checked with the available evidence. If that cannot be tested, report the evidence gap; do not treat a known limitation in the contract as proof that arbitrary additions are scientifically valid.

The controller starts each probe from a fresh copy of the reference outputs at /case/submission. Your script is Python, executed offline with the pinned environment in that directory, which is already the output root. Resolve the declared relative output paths directly there, as described by artifact_interface; do not prepend outputs/. The controller separately tests an extra output-directory layer. Modify only these copied output files. Do not touch grading assets or expected references, inspect other processes, invoke another interpreter, or create background processes. No original biological inputs or scientific rerun are needed here. A probe must exit 0 and change at least one output; no-op scripts, syntax/import errors and grader crashes cannot establish a scientific counterexample. Record changes through the files, not a claimed score. Before accepting your suite, the controller runs each submitted script on fresh copied outputs and checks successful execution and an actual mutation. This preflight does not run or expose the grader. If a script fails, repair the script using that execution evidence; preserve its intended challenge. Only after this preflight are the scripts frozen and evaluated against the grader. Preflight checks execution and mutation, not whether the resulting submission meets the task contract. A deliberate deletion or rename is a mutation; the grader determines whether that submission is acceptable. Prefer scientific mutations over redundant missing-file controls.

Wrong-result controls should remain plausible, parseable outputs whenever the intended defect is scientific: incorrect identities, result values, assignments, rankings or cross-file associations, rather than merely deleting a file. The controller separately checks empty and missing-file submissions. Where outputs contain scientific values or associations, include a wrong-value or wrong-association probe that preserves record identities and row counts; extra/missing records alone do not test value correctness. Choose each edit from inspected evidence and ensure any assertions are true for that edit before submission. Valid alternatives must preserve the public contract; format/order changes establish representation handling only, not independent biological recomputation or software portability. At least one valid representation alternative is required. If no such case can be justified, explain the blocker instead of inventing an equivalence.

For wrong_solution probes, check_ids lists checks expected to fail; each must actually fail for the control to count. For valid_alternative probes, all grader checks must pass. Your controls are frozen before the grader is repaired. Do not make them easier just because the implementation rejects or accepts them incorrectly.

List only checks necessarily violated by the intended edit, as justified by the public rule. Changing an artifact does not imply every check involving it fails: identities, ordering or relations between consistently edited files may remain valid. Do not copy all check IDs associated with a modified file. Explain which scientific requirement the mutation violates and which relations it preserves.

If blocked, submit disposition: "blocked" and explain the evidence gap in the private rationale/concerns. Ready artifacts use disposition: "ready". A blocked submission stops this stage; do not fabricate a candidate just to fill the schema.

Make probe scripts deterministic: choose explicit records and fixed perturbations, and seed any randomness. The controller records the script, input identities, mutated artifact hashes and grader report; a probe must be reproducible from those inputs.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

Recovery from an invalid mutation script

If prior_probe_draft is supplied, the shell is unavailable. Reuse the recorded suite and its cited observations; correct execution errors and fill missing scientific-value coverage. Do not invent new measured observations or claim that prior local checks establish controller acceptance. Submission preflight provides execution-only feedback. Preserve the intended scientific challenges, and do not relax them to accommodate a grader result. Report a blocker if the available observations cannot support a sound repaired suite.
